lines: Rules of the Road: the module that needs 90%
15 lessons, Rules 1 through 38 and the annexes
A short lesson check after every lesson

slides.heading: Picture this

lines: 5:30 a.m.: you leave the dock in Tampa Bay
You run out past Egmont Key into the Gulf
Somewhere on that run, the rules changed

slides.video: Drone shot: a charter boat running down Tampa Bay at dawn and out past Egmont Key.
slides.script: Let’s start with a picture. [+] It’s five-thirty in the morning, and you’re leaving the dock in Tampa Bay with four anglers aboard. [+] You run down the bay, out past Egmont Key, and into the open Gulf to fish a ledge. [+] Here’s my question. Somewhere on that run, the rules you were following changed. Did you notice? [pause] Most captains never do, because the differences are small. But they’re real, and the exam loves them. In the bay, you were under the Inland rules. Out in the Gulf, you were under the International rules. So let’s find that line.

slides.heading: Two sets of rules

head: International (COLREGS)
Inland
rows: High seas and connected waters, seaward of the demarcation lines
U.S. inland waters, shoreward of the demarcation lines
All vessels on U.S. inland waters, and U.S. vessels on Canadian Great Lakes waters

slides.video: Chart close-up: a dashed magenta COLREGS demarcation line across a Florida inlet.
slides.script: There are two rule books, and they’re mostly identical. [+] The International rules, usually called the COLREGS, govern the high seas and the waters connected to them. [+] They come from a 1972 treaty, while the Inland rules are American law, covering our harbors, bays, rivers and the Intracoastal Waterway. [+] Each set applies to every vessel on its waters, whatever flag she flies. [pause] So where’s the line? It’s called the COLREGS demarcation line, and it’s printed on your chart as a dashed magenta line, usually stretched across the mouth of a harbor or inlet. In Florida, you cross it every time you head out an inlet. Here’s some homework: find it on your local chart this week. It makes all of this real.

slides.heading: Rule 1: what can sit alongside the rules

items: Special local rules for harbors, rivers and lakes, conforming as closely as possible
Extra station or signal lights for warships, convoys and fishing fleets
Traffic separation schemes adopted by IMO
Vessels of special construction comply as closely as possible

slides.video: Navy ship at a Florida port at dusk, showing unusual extra lights.
slides.script: Rule one also tells you what can sit alongside these rules, and there are four things to know. [+] First, local authorities can make special rules for a particular harbor, river or lake. But those rules must conform as closely as possible to the Navigation Rules. They can add to them, not throw them out. [+] Second, governments can allow extra lights and shapes for warships, convoys, and fishing fleets working together, and extra whistle signals for warships and convoys. So if you see an odd light on a Navy ship, that’s why. [+] Third, traffic separation schemes, the highway lanes for big ships, are adopted internationally. We’ll cover them in lesson four. [+] And fourth, a vessel of unusual construction that can’t place her lights exactly as required may use the closest alternative her government approves. Inland, that’s called a certificate of alternative compliance.

slides.heading: Rule 2: the rule above all rules

items: No rule excuses neglect of ordinary seamanship
Have due regard to all dangers and special circumstances
Depart from the rules when needed to avoid immediate danger
The rules say who keeps clear, not who has a “right of way”

slides.video: A tug pushing a barge in a channel while a small boat holds course toward it, then turns away.
slides.script: Now, Rule two. If you remember only one rule from this whole course, make it this one. [+] Rule two says nothing in the rules excuses you from the consequences of neglecting ordinary seamanship. In plain English: the rule book is not a shield. [+] You must pay attention to every danger and every special circumstance, including what the other boat can and can’t do. [+] And sometimes, to avoid immediate danger, you have to depart from the rules. That isn’t just allowed, it’s expected. [pause] Here’s how I think about it. Picture yourself as the stand-on boat, holding your course, while a tug pushing a barge clearly isn’t turning. If you hold your course right into that barge, you followed the rules, and you’ll still be found at fault. [+] Notice too that the rules almost never say right of way. They say who keeps out of the way, and who stands on. That’s a mindset, not a privilege.

slides.heading: The annexes

head: Annex
Covers
rows: Positioning and technical details of lights and shapes
International: extra signals for fishing vessels fishing close together. Inland: now in Rule 26
Technical details of sound signal appliances
Inland only: pilot rules, covering law enforcement lights and public safety activities

slides.video: Montage: a masthead light being mounted, a ship’s whistle, a red hand flare, a law enforcement boat’s blue light.
slides.script: The rules end with annexes, and yes, the exam asks about them. Let me give you a one-line handle on each. [+] Annex one is the engineering annex: exactly where lights go, how far apart, how bright. [+] Annex two covers extra signals for fishing boats working close together, like trawlers in a fleet. That annex is International only. In the Inland rules, the same signals now sit inside Rule twenty-six, and Annex two is left empty. [+] Annex three is the technical spec for whistles, bells and gongs. [+] Annex four is the big one for you: distress signals. We’ll spend real time on those in lesson fourteen. [+] And the Inland rules add Annex five, the pilot rules, which cover the blue lights on law enforcement boats and public safety activities.

slides.heading: Four exam habits

items: Find INLAND, INTERNATIONAL or BOTH first
“In sight of one another” or restricted visibility?
Choose the answer that matches the rule’s wording

slides.video: Close-up of a pencil circling the word INLAND on a printed exam question.
slides.script: Before we move on, here are four habits that will save you points on every rules question. [+] First, find the word Inland, International or Both at the start of the question, and answer for that rule book. Circle it if you’re on paper. [+] Second, watch vessel lengths. Seven, twelve, twenty, fifty and one hundred meters are the magic numbers, and rules change at each one. [+] Third, ask yourself: are these boats in sight of each other, or are we in fog? Different rules apply, and you’ll see why in lesson eight. [+] And fourth, when two answers both sound reasonable, pick the one that matches the rule’s actual wording. The exam is written straight from the rule book, not from what people do at the dock. [pause] That’s lesson one. Next, we’ll nail down the definitions, the vocabulary every other rule depends on.

slides.heading: Why definitions matter

lines: Every rule depends on Rule 3’s definitions
Many exam questions are definitions in disguise
Get these right and later lessons get easier

slides.video: Instructor at the helm, Rule 3 text visible in the handbook on the console.
slides.script: Today’s lesson might sound dry, definitions, but stay with me, because this is where a lot of easy points live. [+] Every rule we’ll study depends on the words defined in Rule three. Is that boat sailing or power-driven? Is she underway? Is she engaged in fishing? [+] A huge number of exam questions are really definition questions in disguise. [+] Get these words right, and every later lesson gets easier. So let’s go through them the way a captain would, with real examples.

Is that boat sailing or power-driven? Is she underway? Is she engaged in fishing? A huge number of exam questions are really definition questions in disguise. Get these words right, and every later lesson gets easier. So let’s go through them the way a captain would, with real examples.

slides.heading: Kinds of vessels

items: Vessel: every watercraft, including non-displacement craft, WIG craft and seaplanes
Sailing vessel: under sail, with any engine not being used
Seaplane: an aircraft designed to maneuver on the water

slides.video: A sailboat motoring out a Florida pass with sails up and engine running.
slides.script: First, what counts as a vessel? [+] Pretty much anything that floats and can carry people or things across the water: boats, ships, barges, hovercraft, even seaplanes and wing-in-ground craft. [+] A power-driven vessel is anything propelled by machinery. Simple. [+] A sailing vessel is under sail, with one important catch: any engine she has must not be in use. [pause] So here’s a classic exam question. A sailboat is heading out the pass with every sail up, and her engine is running to help her along. What is she? [pause] She’s a power-driven vessel. The moment that engine turns the prop, the rules treat her like any other powerboat. [+] And a seaplane is simply an aircraft designed to maneuver on the water.

A sailboat is heading out the pass with every sail up, and her engine is running to help her along. What is she? She’s a power-driven vessel. The moment that engine turns the prop, the rules treat her like any other powerboat. And a seaplane is simply an aircraft designed to maneuver on the water.

slides.heading: “Engaged in fishing”

items: Nets, lines, trawls or other gear that restrict maneuverability
A charter boat trolling or drifting with rods out is power-driven
A trawler heading home with gear stowed is power-driven
Anchored with clients’ rods out: still not “engaged in fishing”

slides.video: Split screen: a charter boat trolling four lines beside a shrimp boat working its nets.
slides.script: Now one that matters to you as a charter captain: engaged in fishing. [+] Under the rules, it means fishing with nets, lines, trawls or other gear that restricts your ability to maneuver. [+] And here’s the key: it does not include trolling lines. [pause] So picture your morning. You’ve got four lines out, trolling for kingfish along the beach. Are you engaged in fishing? [+] No. Legally you’re just a power-driven vessel. You get no special privileges, and you keep clear of sailboats like any other powerboat. [+] Meanwhile, the shrimp boat working her nets nearby is engaged in fishing. But when that same shrimper stows her nets and heads home, she’s an ordinary power-driven vessel too. [+] And what if you’re anchored over a wreck with your clients’ lines down? Same answer. Rods and reels don’t restrict your ability to maneuver, so you’re simply a power-driven vessel at anchor. You show anchor lights, not fishing lights. It’s about what the gear is doing, not what kind of boat it is. It isn’t about commercial or recreational either. The only test is whether the gear restricts her maneuverability.

slides.heading: Broken or busy?

head: Not under command
Restricted in ability to maneuver
rows: Dredging; buoy, cable or pipeline work; surveying; diving; a tow that limits her course

slides.video: A disabled sportfisher drifting with no power, then a dredge working in a channel.
slides.script: These two get mixed up all the time, so let’s separate them. [+] Not under command is about cause: some exceptional circumstance, like a failed engine or a jammed rudder, means the vessel can’t maneuver as the rules require. [+] So the word to remember is broken. [+] Restricted in her ability to maneuver is about work: the job she’s doing keeps her from getting out of the way. Dredging, laying cable, servicing a buoy, diving operations, surveying, or a tow that pins her to her course. [pause] Here’s my trick. Ask yourself: is she broken, or is she busy? Broken means not under command. Busy means restricted.

Broken means not under command. Busy means restricted.

slides.heading: Underway, or making way?

items: Constrained by draft: International only; a big ship limited by depth and channel width
Underway: not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground
Making way: moving through the water under her own power
Drifting over a wreck: underway, but not making way

slides.video: A charter boat drifting with engines off over a wreck, anglers bottom fishing.
slides.script: Next, a category that only exists offshore. [+] Constrained by her draft is International only. It’s a big ship whose draft, compared with the depth and width of the water, means she really can’t deviate from her course. You won’t find it in the Inland rules at all. [+] Now, underway. A vessel is underway if she’s not at anchor, not made fast to the shore, and not aground. [+] Making way means actually moving through the water under her own power. [pause] So imagine you shut down to drift over a wreck. You’re not anchored, not tied up, and not aground. [+] You’re underway, but not making way. As you’ll see later, both your lights and your fog signals depend on that difference.

So imagine you shut down to drift over a wreck. You’re not anchored, not tied up, and not aground. You’re underway, but not making way. As you’ll see later, both your lights and your fog signals depend on that difference.

slides.heading: In sight, and visibility

items: Length and breadth: length overall and greatest breadth
In sight of one another: seen with the eyes, not electronics
Restricted visibility: fog, mist, snow, heavy rain, sandstorms; not darkness
A radar or AIS contact in fog is NOT “in sight”

slides.video: A radar screen showing a target in fog, then the same boat emerging from the fog.
slides.script: A few more precise phrases. [+] Length and breadth mean length overall and greatest breadth. Nothing fancy. [+] In sight of one another means one vessel can actually be seen visually from the other. Eyes, not electronics. [+] Restricted visibility means visibility reduced by fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rain, sandstorms or anything similar. Notice what’s not on that list: darkness. A clear night is not restricted visibility. [+] And here’s the one that catches people. If you see a target on your radar or AIS in thick fog, you are not in sight of that vessel. That single fact decides which steering rules apply, and we’ll lean on it heavily in lesson eight.

slides.heading: Inland-only definitions

items: Inland waters: navigable U.S. waters shoreward of the demarcation lines
Great Lakes: including connecting and tributary waters
Western Rivers: the Mississippi system, with the Atchafalaya and Red Rivers
When a question names these waters, expect a special rule

slides.video: Map animation highlighting U.S. inland waters, the Great Lakes and the Mississippi river system.
slides.script: Finally, the Inland rules add a few definitions of their own. [+] Inland waters are the navigable waters of the United States shoreward of the demarcation lines. [+] The Great Lakes include their connecting and tributary waters. [+] The Western Rivers are the Mississippi River system, including the Atchafalaya and the Red River. [+] When a question mentions any of these places, expect a special rule. You may never run a charter on the Mississippi, but the exam will still ask about it. [pause] That’s our vocabulary. Next, we’ll put it to work with the duties every vessel has in any visibility: lookout, safe speed, and judging the risk of collision.

lessons.title: Lookout, safe speed and risk of collision

slides.heading: The lookout

items: Rules 4 to 10 apply in any condition of visibility
Lookout by sight and hearing, at all times
Use every available means: radar, AIS, radio
Goal: a full appraisal of the situation and the risk

slides.video: A busy charter cockpit: fish on, lines tangled, and the captain glancing forward.
slides.script: Let’s start with the duty that shows up in nearly every collision report: the lookout. [+] Rules four through ten apply in any visibility, clear or foggy, day or night. [+] Rule five says every vessel shall at all times keep a proper lookout, by sight and by hearing. [+] And by all available means. If you have radar, AIS and a VHF, they’re part of your lookout. [+] The goal is a full appraisal of the situation and the risk of collision. [pause] Now be honest with yourself. On a busy charter, with a fish on, a tangled line, and a customer asking a question, who’s keeping the lookout? If the answer is nobody, that’s exactly the gap where accidents happen.

slides.heading: Rule 6: safe speed

items: Your stopping distance and turning ability
Wind, sea, current and nearby hazards

slides.video: Night view from a helm: a boat’s running lights almost lost against the condo lights of Clearwater Beach.
slides.script: Rule six is safe speed, and the first thing to know is that there’s no number in it. Safe speed means you can take proper action to avoid a collision, and stop within a distance that fits the conditions. So you weigh the factors. [+] Visibility, obviously. [+] Traffic density, including clusters of fishing boats. [+] Your own boat’s maneuverability: how fast she stops, how tightly she turns. [+] At night, background lights. Try picking out a running light against the condo lights of Clearwater Beach. [+] The state of the wind, sea and current, and nearby hazards. [+] And your draft compared to the depth of the water. [pause] Twenty knots might be perfectly safe in the open Gulf at noon, and reckless in the Intracoastal at dusk.

slides.heading: Safe speed with radar

items: Limits of the range scale in use
Sea state, rain and interference hiding targets
Small boats and floating objects may go undetected
How many vessels radar shows, and how they move
A better measure of visibility, using radar ranges

slides.video: Radar display with sea clutter turned up, hiding a small boat target, then clutter reduced.
slides.script: If you have radar, Rule six adds six more factors, and they boil down to one idea: radar is a tool with limits. [+] Know your radar’s characteristics, efficiency and limitations. [+] Know what the range scale you’ve selected can and can’t show you. [+] Sea state, rain and interference can hide targets in clutter. [+] Small boats, logs and other floating objects may not show up until they’re close. [+] Radar tells you how many vessels are around and how they’re moving. [+] And it can give you a more exact measure of visibility, by showing how far away that boat is that you can just barely see. [pause] The exam trap is assuming radar lets you go faster. It doesn’t. It just gives you better information for judging what’s safe.

slides.heading: Rule 7: is there a risk of collision?
slides.video: Bow-mounted camera: another boat holding the same spot against the windshield frame as it grows larger.
slides.script: Rule seven is about one question: is there a risk of collision? And it starts with a powerful sentence: if there’s any doubt, the risk shall be deemed to exist. Doubt means yes. [pause] So how do you judge it? Look at the diagram. You’re the boat at the bottom, heading up the page, and another boat is crossing from your right. Each dashed line is a bearing taken a minute or so apart. See how the lines stay parallel? The bearing isn’t changing, while the distance shrinks. That’s the classic sign of a collision course. [pause] You can do this with your eyes, too. Line the other boat up with a stanchion or a corner of your windshield. If it stays in that spot while it gets bigger, you’re on a collision course. One warning: with a very large ship, a tow, or anything very close, risk can exist even when the bearing is changing.
slides.spoken: Rule seven is about one question: is there a risk of collision? And it starts with a powerful sentence: if there’s any doubt, the risk shall be deemed to exist. Doubt means yes. So how do you judge it? Look at the diagram. You’re the boat at the bottom, heading up the page, and another boat is crossing from your right. Each dashed line is a bearing taken a minute or so apart. See how the lines stay parallel? The bearing isn’t changing, while the distance shrinks. That’s the classic sign of a collision course. You can do this with your eyes, too. Line the other boat up with a stanchion or a corner of your windshield. If it stays in that spot while it gets bigger, you’re on a collision course. One warning: with a very large ship, a tow, or anything very close, risk can exist even when the bearing is changing.

slides.heading: Captain’s example: one glance isn’t enough

lines: Fog off Port Everglades
One radar glance: a target 3 miles ahead
Plot it for a few minutes before you decide

slides.video: Fog over the Port Everglades entrance; radar screen with a target being marked every minute.
slides.script: Rule seven also covers radar, so here’s a scenario. [+] Imagine you’re heading out of Port Everglades on a rare foggy morning. [+] You glance at the radar and see a target about three miles ahead. One look tells you almost nothing: where it’s going, how fast, whether it’ll pass clear. [+] Rule seven says radar must be used properly, with long-range scanning for early warning, and radar plotting or equivalent systematic observation. Mark the target, watch it for a few minutes, and see how it moves. [pause] And the rule adds a sentence worth memorizing: assumptions shall not be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information. One glance is scanty. A plot is information.

slides.heading: Rule 8: how to act

items: Positive, made in ample time, with good seamanship
Large enough to be obvious by eye or radar
Avoid a series of small alterations
A course change alone may be best, if early, substantial and safe

slides.video: Overhead drone: one boat makes a bold 40-degree turn while another weaves with small course changes.
slides.script: Once you’ve decided there’s a risk, Rule eight tells you how to act. [+] Your action should be positive, made in ample time, and with good seamanship. [+] It should be big enough to be obvious, whether the other captain is watching with his eyes or on radar. A five degree nudge is invisible. A forty degree turn tells a story. [+] Which is why the rule says to avoid a series of small alterations. [+] And if you have sea room, a course change alone is often your best move, as long as it’s early, substantial, and doesn’t just set you up for another close call with someone else. [pause] Think of it like driving: signal clearly, commit, and don’t weave.

slides.heading: Passing clear, and “not to impede”

items: Pass at a safe distance; keep checking until finally past and clear
Slow, stop or back down to buy time
“Not to impede”: act early to leave plenty of room
That duty continues even when risk of collision develops

slides.video: A small boat slowing and turning early to give a ship in the channel plenty of room.
slides.script: Two more parts of Rule eight. [+] Your action must get you past at a safe distance, and you keep checking that it’s working until the other vessel is finally past and clear. [+] If you need more time to figure things out, slow down, stop, or back down. Slowing down is always on the menu, and it buys you time. [+] Rule eight also defines a phrase you’ll meet again and again: not to impede. A vessel required not to impede another must act early, leaving plenty of room. [+] And that duty doesn’t disappear just because the boats get close and a risk of collision develops. [pause] That’s lesson three. Next time, we’ll head into narrow channels and the big-ship highways called traffic separation schemes, where small boats like ours have special duties.

lessons.title: Narrow channels and traffic separation schemes

slides.heading: Rule 9: keep to starboard, don’t impede
slides.script: Today we head into the tightest water you’ll run: narrow channels. Think of the dredged ship channel into Tampa Bay, or the cut at Port Everglades. Rule nine is the rule for these places, and it starts simply. [pause] A vessel following a narrow channel keeps as near to the outer edge on her starboard side as is safe and practicable. In other words, stay to the right, just like on the road. So when two boats meet in a channel, each holds her own right side, and they pass port to port. Now look at the diagram, and find the small boat off to the side. Here’s the part that matters most to you. A vessel of less than twenty meters, or any sailing vessel, shall not impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel. Your charter boat is well under twenty meters. That ship coming down the channel can’t go anywhere else. You can. So you give her room, and you do it early.

slides.heading: Fishing, crossing and anchoring in channels

items: Fishing vessels shall not impede any vessel navigating within the channel
Don’t cross if it impedes a vessel that must stay in the channel
That vessel may sound the danger signal if in doubt
Avoid anchoring in a narrow channel

els: Crossing? Wait for her to pass

slides.script: Rule nine has three more duties, and every one of them applies to a charter boat. [+] First, a vessel engaged in fishing shall not impede any other vessel navigating within a narrow channel. Notice that word, any. Even a true fishing vessel with her nets down gives way to channel traffic here. [+] Second, crossing. You must not cross a narrow channel if crossing would impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within it. So picture this. You’re on one side of the ship channel, the bite is on the other side, and a tanker is coming down. Do you dart across her bow? [pause] No. You wait. [+] And if that ship’s captain is in doubt about what you’re doing, he’ll tell you with the danger signal: at least five short blasts. If you ever hear five short blasts from a ship, assume they’re meant for you. [+] Third, every vessel shall avoid anchoring in a narrow channel, if the circumstances allow. Anchoring up to fish in the ship channel is exactly what this rule is written for.

slides.heading: Overtaking and bends

items: Overtaking that needs the other vessel’s help requires signals and agreement
The vessel being overtaken acts to permit safe passing
Rule 13 still makes the overtaking vessel keep clear
Blind bend: one prolonged blast, answered by one prolonged blast
One prolonged blast, answered by one prolonged blast
If she must help you pass, signal and get agreement

slides.script: Now, overtaking in a channel. Out in open water, you can pass another boat without asking her for anything. In a narrow channel, sometimes you can’t get by unless she moves over. [+] When that’s the case, the overtaking vessel signals her intention with the whistle signals from Rule thirty-four. We’ll learn those signals in lesson thirteen. [+] The vessel being overtaken, if she agrees, answers and takes steps to permit safe passing. If she’s in doubt, she sounds the danger signal instead, and you stay behind her. [+] And here’s the exam point. Even after she agrees, Rule thirteen still applies. The overtaking vessel keeps clear until she’s past. Agreement is permission to pass, not a transfer of responsibility. [pause] [+] One more piece: bends. When you’re nearing a bend, or any spot where something could hide another vessel, navigate with particular alertness and caution, and sound one prolonged blast. Any vessel around the bend that hears you answers with one prolonged blast of her own. Remember it this way: one long blast says, I’m coming around the corner.

slides.heading: Inland Rule 9: downbound vessels

items: Great Lakes, Western Rivers and specified waters only
A downbound power-driven vessel with a following current has right of way
She proposes the manner and place of passage
The upbound vessel holds as necessary to permit safe passing

slides.script: Here’s where the two rule books split, and it’s a favorite exam question. [+] The Inland version of Rule nine adds a special rule for the Great Lakes, the Western Rivers, and other waters the Coast Guard specifies. You won’t find it in the International rules. [+] On those waters, a power-driven vessel heading downbound with a following current has the right of way over an upbound vessel. Yes, right of way. This is one of the very few places where the rules actually use those words. [+] The downbound vessel proposes the manner and place of passage. [+] And she initiates the maneuvering signals. [+] The upbound vessel, the one working against the current, holds as necessary to permit safe passing. Why? Think about a towboat pushing barges down the Mississippi with the current behind her. Can she stop? Can she hold still and wait? [pause] She can’t. The current is carrying her along. The upbound boat can simply ease her throttles and hold her place. So the vessel with less control gets the say. You may never run a river, but when a question says downbound with a following current, you’ll know who’s in charge.

slides.heading: Rule 10: traffic separation schemes
slides.script: On to Rule ten, traffic separation schemes. Picture a divided highway laid out on the water. Look at the diagram: a lane for each direction, with a separation zone between them like a median. You’ll find these off busy ports and in crowded straits, and they’re built for the big ships. But the rule binds everyone who goes near them. If you use a scheme, travel in the proper lane, in the general direction of traffic for that lane. Keep clear of the separation line or zone. Join or leave at the end of a lane when you can. And if you have to come in from the side, do it at as small an angle as practicable, the way you merge onto an interstate. [pause] Crossing is the opposite. Avoid crossing the lanes if you can. But if you’re obliged to cross, do it on a heading as close as practicable to a right angle to the traffic flow. Here’s the trick for keeping them straight. Merge at a small angle. Cross at a right angle. And one more thing: a scheme doesn’t excuse anyone from the other rules. They all still apply inside it.

slides.heading: Rule 10: who uses what

items: Through traffic stays out of inshore traffic zones
Under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels may use inshore zones
Under 20 m and sailing vessels don’t impede power vessels in a lane
Fishing vessels don’t impede vessels following a lane
Avoid anchoring in a scheme or near its ends
Not using the scheme? Avoid it by a wide margin

els: Under 20 m, sailing and fishing vessels may use it

slides.script: So who goes where? [+] Through traffic doesn’t use the inshore traffic zone when it can safely use the lane next to it. The inshore zone is for local traffic. [+] But there are exceptions, and you’re one of them. Vessels of less than twenty meters, sailing vessels, and vessels engaged in fishing may use the inshore zone. So may any vessel going to or from a place inside it, or avoiding immediate danger. [+] Now the duties. A vessel of less than twenty meters, or a sailing vessel, shall not impede the safe passage of a power-driven vessel following a lane. [+] And a vessel engaged in fishing shall not impede any vessel following a lane. Sound familiar? It’s the same idea as Rule nine: small boats, sailboats and fishing boats stay out of the big ships’ way. [+] Avoid anchoring in a scheme, or near its ends. [+] And if you’re not using the scheme, avoid it by as wide a margin as practicable. [pause] Let’s wrap up. In a narrow channel: keep right, don’t impede, don’t cross in front of a ship, and don’t anchor. On the rivers, downbound with a following current is in charge. In a traffic scheme, merge at a small angle, cross at a right angle, and leave the lanes to the ships. Next time, we’ll take up the first of the steering rules: sailing vessels meeting each other, and what the rules mean by overtaking.

slides.heading: Rule 11: vessels in sight

items: Rules 11 to 18 apply only to vessels in sight of one another
In restricted visibility and not in sight, Rule 19 applies instead
Radar contact alone doesn’t make vessels “in sight”

a: The steering and sailing rules for vessels that can see each other
b: Restricted visibility. A radar contact alone isn’t “in sight”

slides.script: Welcome back. Today we start the steering rules proper: who keeps out of whose way. But before any of them, Rule eleven sets a condition, and it’s one sentence long. [+] Rules eleven through eighteen apply only to vessels in sight of one another. Remember that phrase from lesson two? In sight means seen with the eyes. [+] So if you’re in fog and the other vessel isn’t in sight, none of today’s rules apply. There’s no stand-on vessel and no give-way vessel. Rule nineteen takes over instead, and we’ll get to it in lesson eight. [+] And a radar contact alone never makes two vessels in sight. Here’s a quick test. You’re running in thick fog, and your radar shows a boat crossing ahead from your right. Are you the give-way vessel? [pause] No. Nobody is. You can’t see her, so the crossing rule doesn’t apply. Hold on to that idea, because the exam asks it a dozen different ways.

slides.heading: Rule 12: two sailing vessels

items: Wind on different sides: the boat with wind on her port side keeps clear
Wind on the same side: the windward boat keeps clear
Port-tack boat can’t tell the other’s tack: she keeps clear
Windward side: opposite the side the mainsail is carried

slides.script: You may never work a sailboat, but you’ll share the water with plenty of them, and Rule twelve is tested. It decides between two sailing vessels, and it comes down to where the wind is. [+] First, when each boat has the wind on a different side, the one with the wind on her port side keeps out of the way. Sailors call that being on port tack. So, port tack keeps clear. [+] Second, when both boats have the wind on the same side, the boat to windward keeps out of the way of the boat to leeward. Windward is the boat closer to where the wind is coming from. [+] Third, the doubt rule. If you have the wind on your port side, and you see a sailboat to windward but can’t tell which side she has the wind on, you keep out of the way. When in doubt, the port-tack boat gives way. [+] And how do you know which side is windward? For this rule, it’s the side opposite to the one where the mainsail is carried. On a square-rigged vessel, it’s the side opposite her largest fore-and-aft sail. [pause] So a boat with her mainsail out to starboard has the wind on her port side. She’s on port tack, and she keeps clear.

slides.heading: Rule 13: overtaking
slides.script: Now the rule that beats almost every other rule: overtaking. Rule thirteen opens with a strong phrase. Notwithstanding anything in Rules four through eighteen, any vessel overtaking any other shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken. Any vessel. Any other. So what counts as overtaking? Look at the diagram. You’re overtaking when you come up on another vessel from a direction more than twenty-two and a half degrees abaft her beam. That’s the shaded zone behind her. [pause] At night, there’s an easy way to know. From that zone, you can see only her sternlight, and neither of her sidelights. One white light ahead of you, and you’re closing on it? You’re overtaking, and you keep clear. And because this rule overrides the others, the kind of boat doesn’t matter. A sailboat overtaking a powerboat keeps clear. A fishing vessel overtaking anyone keeps clear.

slides.heading: Overtaking: the fine print

items: A later change of bearing doesn’t make it a crossing
Keep clear until finally past and clear

slides.script: Rule thirteen has some fine print, and the exam loves it. [+] First, if you’re in any doubt whether you’re overtaking, assume that you are, and act accordingly. Doubt means keep clear. [+] Second, once you’re overtaking, you stay the overtaking vessel. Any later change in the bearing between the two boats doesn’t turn it into a crossing situation. So picture this. You come up astern of a slow cruiser off Clearwater. As you pull alongside, she’s on your beam, on your port side. In a crossing situation, a boat on your port side would have to keep clear of you. Does that make you the stand-on vessel now? [pause] No. You started as the overtaking vessel, and you’re still the overtaking vessel. [+] You keep clear until you’re finally past and clear. Notice those words. Getting your bow just ahead of hers isn’t enough. [+] And remember the opening phrase: overtaking overrides everything in Rules four through eighteen.

slides.heading: Overtaking meets the pecking order

items: Power overtaking sail: power keeps clear
Sail overtaking power: sail keeps clear
Fishing vessel overtaking anyone: the fishing vessel keeps clear
Coming up from astern? The overtaking vessel keeps clear

slides.script: Let’s test Rule thirteen against the pecking order. You’ll meet that properly in lesson seven, but the short version is that power normally gives way to sail, and sail gives way to vessels engaged in fishing. [+] So, a powerboat overtaking a sailboat. Who keeps clear? The powerboat. Both rules agree, so that one’s easy. [+] Now flip it. A sailboat, flying along in a good breeze, comes up astern of a slow powerboat. Who keeps clear? [pause] The sailboat. She’s overtaking, and overtaking overrides the pecking order. [+] It’s the same with a fishing vessel overtaking anyone. She keeps clear. [+] So here’s your exam habit. Whenever a question describes one vessel coming up on another from astern, stop looking at what kind of vessels they are. The overtaking vessel keeps clear. Every time. [pause] That’s lesson five. The steering rules apply only in sight. Between sailboats, port tack and the windward boat keep clear. And anyone overtaking keeps clear until she’s finally past. Next time, we’ll cover the two situations you’ll meet most often in a powerboat: head-on and crossing.

slides.heading: Rule 14: head-on
slides.script: Today’s lesson covers the two situations you’ll face most in a powerboat, plus the duties that go with them. We start with the simplest: head-on. Rule fourteen applies when two power-driven vessels meet on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses, with a risk of collision. Look at the diagram. What does each boat do? [pause] Each alters course to starboard, so they pass port to port. Both of them. In a head-on situation, there’s no stand-on vessel. How do you know you’re head-on? You see the other vessel ahead, or nearly ahead. At night, you’d see her masthead lights in a line, or nearly in a line, or both of her sidelights at once. Red and green together, coming at you, means turn right. And if you’re in any doubt whether it’s a head-on situation, assume that it is, and act accordingly. Here’s a memory hook: when you meet, go right, and show her your red.

slides.heading: Inland: rivers

items: Great Lakes, Western Rivers and specified waters only
Meeting: a downbound power vessel with a following current has right of way
She proposes the manner of passage and initiates the signals
A power vessel crossing a river keeps clear of power vessels going up or down it

slides.script: The Inland rules add two river rules here, and they belong together. [+] Both apply only on the Great Lakes, the Western Rivers, and other waters the Coast Guard specifies. [+] First, meeting. You saw this in lesson four for narrow channels, and Rule fourteen repeats it. A power-driven vessel heading downbound with a following current has the right of way over an upbound vessel. [+] She proposes the manner of passage, and she initiates the maneuvering signals. [+] Second, crossing. On those same waters, a power-driven vessel crossing a river keeps out of the way of a power-driven vessel going up or down it. It doesn’t matter which side she’s on. Think of a ferry crossing the Mississippi. A towboat is coming down the river on the ferry’s port side. Under the ordinary crossing rule, who would give way? [pause] The towboat would, because the ferry is on her starboard side. But this is a river, so the ferry keeps clear. The traffic running the river comes first.

slides.heading: Rule 15: crossing
slides.script: Now the crossing situation, Rule fifteen, and it’s the one you’ll use every single day. Two power-driven vessels are crossing, with a risk of collision. Which one keeps out of the way? The vessel that has the other on her own starboard side. Look at the diagram. The lower boat sees the other boat off to her right. So she’s the give-way vessel. And the rule adds one more thing: if the circumstances allow, she avoids crossing ahead of the other vessel. So her best move is usually a clear turn to starboard, passing behind the other boat. [pause] Here’s the memory trick, and it works at night. If you’re looking at the other boat’s red sidelight, red means stop. You’re the give-way vessel. If you’re looking at her green sidelight, green means go. You’re the stand-on vessel, and you hold your course and speed. Red, give way. Green, stand on. Just remember that it only works for two power-driven vessels in sight of each other.

slides.heading: Rules 16 and 17: the duties

head: Stage
Stand-on vessel
rows: MAY act by her own maneuver alone
Give-way vessel alone can’t avoid collision
SHALL take the action that best aids to avoid collision

slides.script: So what are the duties? Rule sixteen is the give-way vessel’s, and it’s short. Take early and substantial action to keep well clear. Early. Substantial. Well clear. Rule seventeen is the stand-on vessel’s, and it comes in three stages. [+] Stage one. When risk of collision develops, the stand-on vessel shall keep her course and speed. That’s not stubbornness. It’s what lets the other captain predict what you’ll do. [+] Stage two. As soon as it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel isn’t taking appropriate action, the stand-on vessel may act to avoid collision by her own maneuver alone. May. It’s allowed, not required. This is the moment for five short blasts. [+] Stage three. When she’s so close that the give-way vessel alone can’t avoid the collision, the stand-on vessel shall take whatever action will best help avoid it. Shall. Now it’s required. [pause] So the pattern is: shall hold, may act, shall act. The exam tests the difference between may and shall, so lock that pattern in.

slides.heading: Rule 17: two more details

items: Crossing: a stand-on power vessel avoids turning to port for a vessel on her own port side
Stand-on action never relieves the give-way vessel
Keep course and speed means predictable, not reckless

els: Don’t turn to port for a vessel on your port side

slides.script: Two more details of Rule seventeen, and then a thought of my own. [+] First, when a power-driven stand-on vessel acts on her own in a crossing situation, she should not, if the circumstances allow, turn to port for a vessel on her own port side. Why not? Picture it. The other boat is on your port side, and she’s late, but she finally turns to starboard to go behind you. If you turn to port at the same moment, you turn straight into her. So turn to starboard, or slow down, or stop. [+] Second, nothing the stand-on vessel does relieves the give-way vessel of her obligation. She’s still responsible for keeping out of the way. [+] And here’s my thought. Keeping your course and speed means being predictable. It doesn’t mean being reckless. Rule two is still there, and no captain was ever praised for standing on into a collision. [pause] That’s lesson six. Head-on: both turn to starboard. Crossing: the boat with the other on her starboard side gives way. And for the stand-on vessel: shall hold, may act, shall act. Next time, we’ll climb the pecking order and see who gives way to whom when the vessels aren’t alike.

slides.heading: Rule 18: the ladder
slides.script: So far, every steering rule has been about two boats of the same kind. Today’s question is different. What happens when a powerboat meets a sailboat, or a sailboat meets a trawler with her nets down? Rule eighteen answers it with what I call the ladder. Look at the screen, and read it from the bottom up. [pause] Each vessel keeps out of the way of the vessels above her. A power-driven vessel underway keeps out of the way of four kinds of vessel: one not under command, one restricted in her ability to maneuver, one engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel. Power-driven sits on the bottom rung, and that’s where your charter boat lives. So here’s the plain truth. Most days, almost everything out there that isn’t another powerboat has priority over you. The logic of the ladder is simple: the less a vessel can maneuver, the higher she stands.

slides.heading: Up the ladder

items: Sailing vessels keep clear of: NUC, RAM, fishing
Fishing vessels keep clear, as far as possible, of: NUC, RAM
NUC and RAM sit at the top
NUC and RAM, as far as possible

slides.script: Let’s climb it one rung at a time. [+] A sailing vessel underway keeps out of the way of three: a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing. So a sailboat gives way to a working trawler. Many sailors forget that one. [+] Next rung. A vessel engaged in fishing, when underway, keeps out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver. But listen to the wording: so far as possible. Her gear limits what she can do, and the rule admits it. [+] And at the top sit the vessel not under command and the vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver. Nobody is listed above them, because by definition they can’t easily get out of anyone’s way. [pause] Remember the trick from lesson two? Broken, or busy. Broken or busy sits at the top. Then fishing, then sail, then power.

slides.heading: Constrained by draft

items: Any vessel except NUC or RAM avoids impeding a CBD vessel
The CBD vessel navigates with particular caution
“Not impeding” means acting early, not stand-on or give-way
The Inland rules have no such vessel

slides.script: There’s one more vessel to place, and she only exists offshore. [+] Constrained by her draft is International only. You won’t find her in the Inland rules. [+] Under the International rules, any vessel other than one not under command, or one restricted in her ability to maneuver, shall, if the circumstances allow, avoid impeding the safe passage of a vessel constrained by her draft. That’s a deep ship in a channel she can’t leave, showing the signals of Rule twenty-eight. [+] In return, the constrained vessel has a duty of her own. She navigates with particular caution, with full regard to her special condition. [+] Now notice the words avoid impeding. Remember from Rule eight what that means? [pause] It means acting early to leave her sea room. It isn’t the same thing as give-way and stand-on. So if an exam question asks who is the stand-on vessel here, be careful. The rule doesn’t use those words.

slides.heading: When the ladder doesn’t apply

items: Rule 9: small and sailing vessels don’t impede ships in a narrow channel
Rule 10: the same applies in traffic lanes
Rule 13: the overtaking vessel always keeps clear
Example: a sailboat in a ship channel must not impede a tanker

els: A sailboat must not impede a tanker in a channel

slides.script: Now for the trap. Rule eighteen opens with six words that the exam loves: except where Rules nine, ten and thirteen otherwise require. So the ladder has three exceptions. [+] Rule nine, narrow channels. A sailing vessel, or any vessel under twenty meters, shall not impede a vessel that can navigate only within the channel. [+] Rule ten, traffic separation schemes. The same idea applies to vessels following a traffic lane. [+] And Rule thirteen, overtaking. The overtaking vessel always keeps clear, whatever she is. [+] So try this one. A sailboat is tacking up the ship channel in Tampa Bay, and a loaded tanker is coming down it. On the ladder, sail stands above power. Who has to stay out of the way? [pause] The sailboat. She must not impede the tanker, because Rule nine overrides the ladder. Here’s your exam habit. Before you apply the ladder, check the question for three things: a narrow channel, a traffic lane, or overtaking.

slides.heading: Seaplanes and WIG craft

items: Seaplane on the water: keep well clear of all vessels
If risk of collision exists, a seaplane follows the steering rules
WIG craft taking off, landing or flying near the surface: keep clear of all vessels
WIG craft on the water: follow the rules as a power-driven vessel
Keeps well clear of all vessels
Keeps well clear of all vessels
Follows the rules as a power-driven vessel

slides.script: Last, two unusual craft that Rule eighteen also covers. [+] A seaplane on the water shall, in general, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation. Think of it this way: she can leave by air, so she stays out of the way on the water. [+] But where risk of collision exists, she follows the steering rules like everyone else. [+] A wing-in-ground craft, when taking off, landing, or flying near the surface, keeps well clear of all other vessels and avoids impeding their navigation. [+] And when she’s operating on the water surface, she follows the rules as a power-driven vessel. [pause] That’s lesson seven. The ladder, from the top: broken or busy, then fishing, then sail, then power. Constrained by draft is International only. And narrow channels, traffic lanes and overtaking override the ladder. Next time, we go where none of this applies: into the fog, and Rule nineteen.

slides.heading: Rule 19: when it applies

items: Vessels not in sight of one another
In or near an area of restricted visibility
Every vessel shares the duty to avoid collision

b: Not in sight, in or near fog
No stand-on vessel. Every vessel must avoid collision

slides.script: Picture a January morning on Tampa Bay. You leave the dock in sunshine, and half a mile out, the world turns white. You can’t see your own bow rail. Which steering rules apply now? [pause] Not the ones we’ve been studying. This is Rule nineteen, and it’s one of the most tested rules in the book. [+] It applies to vessels not in sight of one another. [+] And it applies when you’re navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility. Notice the words or near. You can be in clear air, running alongside a fog bank, and Rule nineteen still applies to you and to whatever is inside that bank. [+] Now the big idea. Under Rule nineteen, there is no stand-on vessel and no give-way vessel. None. The crossing rule, the head-on rule and the ladder are all switched off. [+] Instead, every vessel shares the same duty to avoid a close-quarters situation. Nobody gets to hold her course and wait for the other boat to act.

slides.heading: Speed and readiness

items: Safe speed adapted to the visibility
Power-driven vessels keep engines ready for immediate maneuver
Apply Rules 4 to 10 with the visibility in mind
Sound fog signals, keep lights on, plot radar targets

slides.script: So what does the rule ask of you? Start with speed and readiness. [+] Every vessel shall proceed at a safe speed adapted to the conditions of restricted visibility. That’s Rule six, with the fog pressed down hard on it. [+] A power-driven vessel shall have her engines ready for immediate maneuver. No autopilot and a cup of coffee. A hand near the throttles. [+] And every vessel applies Rules four through ten with the visibility in mind: the lookout, safe speed, risk of collision, and action to avoid it. [+] So here’s what that looks like on your boat. Slow down. Put someone forward to listen, away from the engine noise. Sound your fog signals. Turn your navigation lights on, even at noon. And if you have radar, plot every target, don’t just glance at it. [pause] One more thing your passengers won’t like: quiet on deck. In fog, your ears are a navigation instrument.

And every vessel applies Rules four through ten with the visibility in mind: the lookout, safe speed, risk of collision, and action to avoid it. So here’s what that looks like on your boat. slides.heading: Radar-only contacts
slides.script: Here’s the heart of Rule nineteen, and it’s for the boat with radar. If you detect another vessel by radar alone, you must work out whether a close-quarters situation is developing, or a risk of collision exists. If it is, you take avoiding action in ample time. And if that action is a change of course, there are two things to avoid, so far as possible. Look at the left picture. First: avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of your beam, unless you’re overtaking her. Now the right picture. Second: avoid altering course toward a vessel that’s abeam or abaft your beam. [pause] Put those together and the pattern is simple. For a target ahead of you, don’t turn left. For a target beside or behind you, don’t turn toward her. So for a vessel ahead, a substantial turn to starboard is usually the safe choice. And slowing down, or stopping, is always allowed.

slides.heading: Hearing a fog signal

items: Hear a fog signal apparently forward of your beam?
Or can’t avoid close quarters with a vessel forward of the beam?
Reduce to the minimum speed that keeps you on course
Take all way off if necessary
Navigate with extreme caution until the danger is over

els: Fog signal forward of your beam?
Stop if you must. Extreme caution until it’s over

slides.script: Now the second half of the rule, and this one is for every vessel, radar or not. It’s about what you hear. [+] Suppose you hear a fog signal, and it seems to come from forward of your beam. [+] Or suppose you simply can’t avoid a close-quarters situation with a vessel forward of your beam. [+] Then you shall reduce your speed to the minimum at which you can keep your course. Bare steerageway. [+] If necessary, you take all your way off. You stop. [+] And in any event, you navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over. The only exception is when you’ve already determined that no risk of collision exists. [pause] Notice one small word in the rule: apparently. The signal is apparently forward of your beam. Why would the rule say that? Because sound plays tricks in fog. It bends, it echoes, and it can seem to come from the wrong direction. So when you hear a horn ahead, don’t guess, and don’t turn. Slow down first.

slides.heading: Handing over to the other rules

items: Once you sight each other, Rules 11 to 18 apply
Radar alone never makes you “in sight”
No assumptions on scanty radar information
Fog signals are in Rule 35, lesson 14

slides.script: Last, how does Rule nineteen hand back to the other rules? [+] The moment two vessels actually sight one another, the rules for vessels in sight take over: Rules eleven through eighteen. A stand-on vessel and a give-way vessel exist again. So picture a boat breaking out of the fog two hundred yards off your starboard bow. You can see her now. You’re in a crossing situation, and you’re the give-way vessel. [+] But radar alone never makes you in sight. [+] And Rule seven’s warning applies with full force here: no assumptions on scanty radar information. [+] The fog signals themselves are in Rule thirty-five, and we’ll learn them in lesson fourteen. [pause] That’s lesson eight. In or near fog, and not in sight, nobody stands on. Radar target ahead: don’t turn to port. Fog signal forward of the beam: slow to bare steerageway, and stop if you must. Next time, we start the lights, beginning with the ones on your own boat.

lessons.title: Lights: arcs, ranges and power-driven vessels

slides.heading: Rule 20: when lights and shapes apply

items: Lights: sunset to sunrise, in all weather
Also in restricted visibility, and whenever necessary
No other lights that could be mistaken for them or spoil the lookout

a: Lights, in all weather. Also by day in restricted visibility

slides.script: Welcome to the lights. For the next four lessons, we’ll learn to read a vessel in the dark: what she is, which way she’s heading, and what she’s doing. It starts with Rule twenty, which tells you when the light rules apply. [+] Lights are shown from sunset to sunrise, and in all weathers. [+] They’re also shown from sunrise to sunset in restricted visibility, and you may show them any other time you think it’s necessary. So in a daytime fog bank or a black squall, your lights go on. [+] During those hours, you show no other lights that could be mistaken for the required ones, that spoil their visibility, or that interfere with keeping a proper lookout. Here’s the one that catches charter captains. Those bright deck lights you rig for night fishing? If they blind your own lookout, or drown out your sidelights, they break this rule. [+] Shapes are the daytime version, and the shape rules apply by day. [+] And the technical details, exactly where each light goes, are in Annex one.
slides.spoken: Welcome to the lights. For the next four lessons, we’ll learn to read a vessel in the dark: what she is, which way she’s heading, and what she’s doing. It starts with Rule twenty, which tells you when the light rules apply. Lights are shown from sunset to sunrise, and in all weathers. They’re also shown from sunrise to sunset in restricted visibility, and you may show them any other time you think it’s necessary. So in a daytime fog bank or a black squall, your lights go on. During those hours, you show no other lights that could be mistaken for the required ones, that spoil their visibility, or that interfere with keeping a proper lookout. Here’s the one that catches charter captains. Those bright deck lights you rig for night fishing? If they blind your own lookout, or drown out your sidelights, they break this rule. Shapes are the daytime version, and the shape rules apply by day. And the technical details, exactly where each light goes, are in Annex one.

slides.heading: Rule 21: the lights defined
slides.script: Before we read anyone else’s lights, we need the vocabulary, and that’s Rule twenty-one. Look at the diagram as I go around the boat. The masthead light is white, on the centerline, and it shines over two hundred twenty-five degrees: from dead ahead to twenty-two and a half degrees abaft the beam on each side. The sidelights are green to starboard and red to port. Each one covers one hundred twelve and a half degrees, from dead ahead to twenty-two and a half degrees abaft the beam on its own side. On a vessel under twenty meters, they can be combined in one lantern. The sternlight is white, and it covers the remaining one hundred thirty-five degrees aft. [pause] Now add them up. Two sidelights make two hundred twenty-five degrees, the same as the masthead light. Add the sternlight’s one hundred thirty-five, and you have the full circle, three hundred sixty. That’s why you see either her sidelights or her sternlight, never both. Three more. A towing light is yellow, with the same arc as a sternlight. An all-round light shows through the full three hundred sixty degrees. And a flashing light flashes one hundred twenty times a minute or more.

slides.heading: Rule 22: visibility ranges (nautical miles)

items: Masthead 5 miles, or 3 if under 20 m

slides.script: Rule twenty-two is pure numbers: how far away each light must be visible. I won’t pretend there’s a way around memorizing it, but there is a pattern. Bigger vessel, brighter lights. Look at the table as it builds. [+] The masthead light is always the strongest. Six miles on a vessel of fifty meters or more. Five miles from twelve to fifty meters, but only three miles if she’s under twenty meters. And two miles under twelve meters. [+] Sidelights: three miles, two miles, and one mile. That one-mile sidelight on a small boat is the shortest range in the whole table. [+] The sternlight: three miles, two, and two. [+] The towing light matches the sternlight: three, two, and two. [+] And all-round lights are the same again: three, two, and two. [pause] So here’s the handle. On a big ship, the masthead is six and everything else is three. In the middle group, the masthead is five, or three under twenty meters, and everything else is two. On a small boat, everything is two, except the sidelights, which are one.

slides.heading: Rule 23: power-driven vessels underway
slides.script: Now let’s put lights on a boat. Rule twenty-three covers a power-driven vessel underway, and she shows a masthead light forward, sidelights, and a sternlight. [+] Here’s a vessel under fifty meters, coming straight at you. You see one white masthead light, with red and green below it. Red and green together means she’s head-on. [+] Now a vessel of fifty meters or more, showing you her starboard side. She must carry a second masthead light, behind the first and higher. A smaller vessel may carry one, but doesn’t have to. Why does it matter? Those two white lights work like a range. The lower one is forward, so it points the way she’s heading. And when the two lights start to close up or open out, she’s turning. [+] And here’s the option for boats under twelve meters: one all-round white light, plus sidelights. That’s probably what’s on your center console right now. [pause] So tonight at the dock, look at your own boat. Which arrangement do you carry?

So tonight at the dock, look at your own boat. Which arrangement do you carry?

slides.heading: Rule 23: special cases

items: Air-cushion vessel, non-displacement mode: all-round flashing yellow
WIG craft near the surface: high-intensity all-round flashing red
Under 7 m with max speed 7 knots: all-round white, sidelights if practicable
Under 12 m: masthead or all-round light may be off the centerline
Inland, Great Lakes: all-round white may replace second masthead light and sternlight
Masthead light may be off the centerline

slides.script: A few special cases to finish, and each one is a favorite exam question. [+] An air-cushion vessel, when she’s operating in the non-displacement mode, adds an all-round flashing yellow light. Hovercraft, flashing yellow. [+] A wing-in-ground craft, when taking off, landing or flying near the surface, adds a high-intensity all-round flashing red light. [+] Next, the smallest powerboats. Under the International rules, a power-driven vessel under seven meters, whose top speed is no more than seven knots, may show just an all-round white light, and sidelights too if practicable. Seven meters, seven knots. [+] On a boat under twelve meters, the masthead light or all-round white light doesn’t have to be exactly on the centerline, if that isn’t practicable. [+] And one for the Inland rules. On the Great Lakes, a power-driven vessel may carry an all-round white light in place of the second masthead light and the sternlight. [pause] That’s lesson nine. Lights from sunset to sunrise and in restricted visibility. Masthead two twenty-five, sidelights one twelve and a half, sternlight one thirty-five. And for ranges, think six and three, five and two, two and one. Next time: the lights of vessels that are towing.

slides.heading: Rule 24: towing astern
slides.script: Florida’s waters are full of tugs: fuel barges on the Intracoastal, dredge pipe in the inlets, big ocean tows off the coast. A tow is the most dangerous thing you can misread at night, because there may be hundreds of feet of cable between the tug and whatever she’s pulling. Rule twenty-four tells you how to spot one. [+] Start from astern. A vessel towing astern shows a yellow towing light directly above her white sternlight. Yellow over white, towing tonight. If you’re coming up behind those two lights, something is trailing behind her, between you and the tug. [+] Now from ahead. A power-driven vessel towing astern shows two masthead lights in a vertical line, plus sidelights. Two white lights stacked means a tow of two hundred meters or less. [+] And when the tow is longer than two hundred meters, she shows three masthead lights in a vertical line. How is that length measured? [pause] From the stern of the towing vessel to the after end of the tow. By day, a tow over two hundred meters is marked with a diamond shape, on both the towing vessel and the tow. And a tug of fifty meters or more still carries her other masthead light as well.

slides.heading: Pushing ahead and towing alongside
slides.script: Not every tow is behind the tug. On the Intracoastal you’ll mostly see barges pushed ahead, or lashed alongside. First, one special case. When a pushing vessel and the vessel she pushes are rigidly connected as a composite unit, they count as one power-driven vessel, and show ordinary Rule twenty-three lights. Otherwise, here’s what you’ll see. [+] From ahead, a vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside shows two masthead lights in a vertical line, and sidelights. [+] From astern is where the two rule books split. Under the International rules, she shows a sternlight. One white light. [+] Under the Inland rules, she shows two yellow towing lights in a vertical line instead. So picture yourself overtaking something big and slow on the Intracoastal at night, and all you see is two yellow lights, one above the other. What is it? [pause] A towboat pushing ahead or towing alongside, under Inland rules. And one more Inland detail: on the Western Rivers and certain other waters, a vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside shows sidelights and the two towing lights, with no masthead lights at all.

slides.heading: Lights on the tow itself
slides.script: Now the other end of the towline: what does the tow itself show? [+] Start with a barge being pushed ahead. Under the International rules, she shows sidelights at her forward end. Under the Inland rules, she shows sidelights and a special flashing light at the forward end. That special flashing light is yellow, it flashes fifty to seventy times a minute, and it shines forward over an arc of between one hundred eighty and two hundred twenty-five degrees. So a flashing yellow light low on the water, with a red and a green beside it, is the front of a pushed barge. And the tug may be a long way behind it. [+] A vessel or object towed astern shows sidelights and a sternlight, just like any vessel without a masthead light, plus a diamond by day if the tow is over two hundred meters. [pause] Two more. A vessel towed alongside shows a sternlight, and sidelights at her forward end. And any number of vessels pushed or towed alongside in a group are lit as if they were one vessel.

Under the Inland rules, she shows sidelights and a special flashing light at the forward end. That special flashing light is yellow, it flashes fifty to seventy times a minute, and it shines forward over an arc of between one hundred eighty and two hundred twenty-five degrees. So a flashing yellow light low on the water, with a red and a green beside it, is the front of a pushed barge. And the tug may be a long way behind it. A vessel or object towed astern shows sidelights and a sternlight, just like any vessel without a masthead light, plus a diamond by day if the tow is over two hundred meters. Two more. A vessel towed alongside shows a sternlight, and sidelights at her forward end. And any number of vessels pushed or towed alongside in a group are lit as if they were one vessel.

slides.heading: Special towing situations

items: A tow that severely restricts her course: add the RAM lights and shapes
Partly submerged objects: all-round white lights at the ends, diamond aft
Can’t light the tow? Take all possible measures to show its presence
Rescue tows needn’t show towing lights if impracticable, but illuminate the towline
Add the RAM lights and shapes
White lights at the ends, a diamond aft
Do everything possible to show it’s there

slides.script: Four special situations to finish the towing rule. [+] First, a tow that severely restricts the tug’s ability to deviate from her course. She adds the lights and shapes of a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, on top of her towing lights. Remember the ladder: that moves her up near the top. [+] Second, things that are hard to see. An inconspicuous, partly submerged vessel or object being towed, like a fuel bladder, shows all-round white lights at its ends, more if it’s very wide, and a diamond shape at the after end. [+] Third, what if the tow simply can’t be lit that way? Then all possible measures shall be taken to light it, or at least to show that it’s there. [+] And fourth, this one is about you. Say a friend’s boat breaks down at dusk and you take her in tow. You’re not a towing vessel, and you don’t carry towing lights. Are you breaking the rule? [pause] No. A vessel not normally engaged in towing needn’t show towing lights when it’s impracticable. But you must show the connection between the two boats, for example by lighting up the towline. That’s lesson ten. Yellow over white from astern, two or three white lights stacked from ahead, and two yellow lights for an Inland pusher. Next time: sailboats and fishing vessels.

slides.heading: Rule 25: sailing vessels
slides.script: Tonight’s lights belong to the two kinds of vessel that stand above you on the ladder: sail and fishing. If you can’t recognize them in the dark, you can’t give way to them. We’ll start with Rule twenty-five, sailing vessels. [+] A sailing vessel underway shows sidelights and a sternlight. And that’s all. What’s missing? [pause] The masthead light. No white light forward. So red and green with no white above them is a boat under sail, coming at you. [+] On a sailing vessel under twenty meters, those three lights can be combined in one lantern at or near the top of the mast. Sailors call it a tricolor. It’s high up, so it shows over the waves. [+] And a sailing vessel may add two all-round lights at or near the masthead: red over green. Red over green, sailing machine. She shows those along with her sidelights and sternlight. But she can’t show them together with the tricolor lantern.

But she can’t show them together with the tricolor lantern.

slides.heading: Small sailboats, rowing and motorsailing

items: Sail under 7 m: sidelights and sternlight if practicable
Otherwise a white torch or lantern, shown in time to prevent collision
Rowing boats: sailing lights, or the white torch
Motorsailing by day: a cone, point down
Inland: under 12 m, that cone is optional
Or a white torch or lantern
Shown in time to prevent collision

slides.script: Now the small stuff, and one daytime shape. [+] A sailing vessel under seven meters shows sidelights and a sternlight if practicable. [+] If she doesn’t, she must have an electric torch or a lighted lantern ready, showing a white light, and show it in enough time to prevent collision. So that single white light waving at you off the beach at dusk may be a little daysailer, telling you she’s there. [+] A vessel under oars may show the sailing lights. If not, she needs that same white torch or lantern ready. [+] Now the shape. By day, a vessel under sail that’s also being propelled by her engine shows a cone, point down, forward where it can best be seen. Why would she bother? [pause] Because with her sails up she looks like a sailboat, but under the rules she’s a power-driven vessel. The cone tells you the truth. [+] And the Inland difference: under the Inland rules, a vessel under twelve meters isn’t required to show that cone, but may.

slides.heading: Rule 26: fishing vessels
slides.script: Rule twenty-six covers vessels engaged in fishing, and remember from lesson two what that means: gear that restricts her maneuverability. These lights apply whether she’s underway or at anchor. [+] A trawler shows two all-round lights: green over white. Green over white, trawling tonight. She also carries a masthead light behind and above the green one, though a trawler under fifty meters doesn’t have to. Off this coast, that’s your shrimp boat. [+] A vessel fishing any other way shows red over white. Red over white, fishing tonight. [+] And when her gear reaches out more than one hundred fifty meters from her, she adds an all-round white light in the direction of the gear. So which side do you pass on? [pause] The other side. Stay away from that white light. One more thing for both kinds. When she’s making way through the water, she adds sidelights and a sternlight. No sidelights means she’s fishing but not making way.

slides.heading: Fishing day shapes

items: Gear over 150 m: cone, point up, toward the gear

slides.script: By day, fishing vessels use shapes. [+] A vessel engaged in fishing shows two cones with their points together, one above the other. It looks like an hourglass. [+] And when her gear extends more than one hundred fifty meters, she adds a single cone, point up, in the direction of the gear. Same idea as the white light at night: it points to where the gear is. [pause] Now the other half of the rule, and it’s a favorite on the exam. When a fishing vessel isn’t engaged in fishing, she shows only the ordinary lights or shapes for a vessel of her length. So think of a shrimper steaming home before dawn with her nets stowed. What does she show? Plain power-driven lights. And what privileges does she have over you? None. She’s just another power-driven vessel.

slides.heading: Annex II: fishing close together

head: Signal
Meaning
rows: Purse seiner hampered by her gear

slides.script: Last, the extra signals for fishing vessels working close together. In the International rules they’re in Annex two. In the Inland rules they now sit inside Rule twenty-six itself. They’re optional, they’re carried lower than the main fishing lights, and they’re visible at least a mile. The exam asks you to match each signal to its meaning, so let’s go down the table. [+] A trawler shooting her nets, putting them out: two white lights in a vertical line. [+] A trawler hauling her nets, bringing them in: white over red. [+] A trawler whose net has come fast on an obstruction: two red lights in a vertical line. Two reds usually means trouble, and here the trouble is a snagged net. [+] Vessels pair trawling may each aim a searchlight forward and toward the other boat of the pair. [+] And a purse seiner hampered by her gear may show two yellow lights in a vertical line, flashing alternately. [pause] That’s lesson eleven. Sail: sidelights and sternlight, no masthead light, and red over green if she likes. Trawling: green over white. Other fishing: red over white. Next time, the vessels at the top of the ladder, and the lights of boats at anchor and aground.

slides.heading: Rule 27: NUC and RAM
slides.script: Today we light the top of the ladder: the broken and the busy. Remember them? Not under command, and restricted in her ability to maneuver. Rule twenty-seven gives each a signal you can’t mistake. [+] A vessel not under command shows two all-round red lights in a vertical line. By day, two balls. Red over red, the captain is dead. It’s a grim little rhyme, but you won’t forget it. In this picture she isn’t making way, so the two red lights are all she shows. [+] When she is making way, she adds sidelights and a sternlight. But no masthead light. [+] A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver shows three all-round lights in a vertical line: red, white, red. By day, a ball, a diamond, and a ball. When she’s making way, she adds masthead lights, sidelights and a sternlight. And at anchor, she shows her restricted lights plus her anchor lights. [pause] So here’s how to read any of these. The special lights tell you her condition. The ordinary lights tell you whether she’s moving.
slides.spoken: Today we light the top of the ladder: the broken and the busy. Remember them? Not under command, and restricted in her ability to maneuver. Rule twenty-seven gives each a signal you can’t mistake. A vessel not under command shows two all-round red lights in a vertical line. By day, two balls. Red over red, the captain is dead. It’s a grim little rhyme, but you won’t forget it. In this picture she isn’t making way, so the two red lights are all she shows. When she is making way, she adds sidelights and a sternlight. But no masthead light. A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver shows three all-round lights in a vertical line: red, white, red. By day, a ball, a diamond, and a ball. When she’s making way, she adds masthead lights, sidelights and a sternlight. And at anchor, she shows her restricted lights plus her anchor lights. So here’s how to read any of these. The special lights tell you her condition. The ordinary lights tell you whether she’s moving.

slides.heading: Dredges and divers

items: Dredge: pass on the green side

slides.script: Dredges work Florida’s inlets and channels all year, and they’re restricted vessels with one extra job: telling you which side is safe. [+] Look at the picture. A vessel dredging or doing underwater work shows her red, white, red lights. Then, on the side where the obstruction is, two all-round red lights in a vertical line, or two balls by day. And on the side where you may pass, two all-round green lights in a vertical line, or two diamonds by day. So which side do you take? [pause] The green side. Green means go, just like a traffic light. Now, diving. A boat engaged in diving operations that’s too small to show all of that shows the red, white, red lights, and a rigid replica of the International Code flag A, at least one meter high, visible all around. In Florida you’ll also see the state’s red and white diver-down flag. Either one means the same thing to you: slow down and stay well clear.

slides.heading: Mine clearance and small vessels

items: Mine clearance: three all-round green lights, or three balls
Under 12 m, except divers: NUC and RAM signals not required
Three all-round green lights, or three balls
These signals mark work, not an emergency

slides.script: A few more points from Rule twenty-seven. [+] A vessel engaged in mine clearance shows three all-round green lights, or three balls by day: one near the foremast head, and one at each end of the fore yard. So they form a triangle, not a line. [+] And they mean it’s dangerous to come within one thousand meters of her. That’s more than half a mile, all the way around. [+] Now a break for small boats. Vessels under twelve meters, except those engaged in diving operations, aren’t required to show the not-under-command or restricted signals. [+] And one thing people get wrong. None of these are distress signals. So suppose you see two red lights, one above the other, on a ship drifting offshore. Is she calling for help? [pause] No. She’s telling you she can’t get out of your way. If she needs help, she’ll use the distress signals in lesson fourteen.

slides.heading: Rules 28 and 29: draft and pilots
slides.script: Two shorter rules now. [+] Rule twenty-eight is International only. A vessel constrained by her draft may show, along with her ordinary power-driven lights, three all-round red lights in a vertical line. By day, a cylinder. You met her on the ladder in lesson seven. And you’ll never see those lights on Inland waters, because that category doesn’t exist there. [+] Rule twenty-nine is the pilot boat. A pilot vessel on pilotage duty shows two all-round lights at or near the masthead: white over red. White over red, pilot ahead. Underway, she adds sidelights and a sternlight. [+] At anchor, she keeps the white over red and adds her anchor light or lights. And when she’s not on pilotage duty, she shows only the ordinary lights for a vessel of her length. [pause] Now be careful with the rhymes, because two of them are mirror images. White over red is a pilot. Red over white is fishing. So ask yourself which color is on top.
