slides.heading: Waves and seas

items: Wave size grows with wind speed, fetch and duration
Fetch: the distance of open water the wind blows across
Swell: waves that have left the area where they formed
Forecast heights are significant wave height: the average of the highest third
Expect some waves much larger, occasionally about double

els: Fetch: open water the wind crosses
More wind, more fetch, more time: bigger waves

slides.script: Waves grow with three things: wind speed; fetch, the distance of open water the wind blows across; and duration, how long it has blown. That’s why an offshore wind leaves a calm strip near the beach, while the same wind blowing onshore across a long fetch builds big seas. Swell is waves that have traveled away from where they formed, and it can arrive well ahead of a distant storm. Forecast wave heights are significant wave heights, the average of the highest one third of the waves, so expect some individual waves much larger, occasionally around twice the forecast height.

lessons.title: Your license and the passenger rules

slides.heading: What the OUPV allows

items: Near Coastal: up to 100 nm offshore; Inland: inside the boundary line
Valid 5 years; renew through the National Maritime Center
7 or more passengers: inspected vessel and a Master license

fig.cap: Up to six passengers for hire, on uninspected vessels
fig.sub: Near Coastal: up to 100 nm offshore

slides.script: Welcome to Deck General and Safety. The Rules module was about not hitting anybody. This one is about everything else it takes to run a safe, legal charter, and it starts with the piece of paper you’re studying for. So what does a six-pack license actually let you do? [+] It lets you carry up to six passengers for hire. That’s where the nickname comes from. [+] And only on an uninspected vessel. [+] Where you can go depends on your endorsement. Near Coastal takes you up to one hundred miles offshore. Inland keeps you inside the boundary line. [+] The credential is good for five years, and you renew it through the National Maritime Center. [+] Now the limit. What if a seventh paying passenger wants to come along? [pause] You can’t take him. Seven or more passengers for hire means an inspected vessel, with a Certificate of Inspection, and a Master license. Six is a hard number.

Now the limit. What if a seventh paying passenger wants to come along? You can’t take him. Seven or more passengers for hire means an inspected vessel, with a Certificate of Inspection, and a Master license. Six is a hard number.

slides.heading: Who is a passenger for hire?

items: A passenger for whom consideration is contributed as a condition of carriage
Consideration: money or any economic benefit, directly or indirectly
Voluntary sharing of the trip’s actual expenses is NOT consideration
Owners, crew and true non-paying guests aren’t passengers for hire
Disguised fees (“donations,” required fuel charges) still count

a: Pays, directly or indirectly, as a condition of the trip
b: Guests, crew, or friends voluntarily sharing actual expenses

slides.script: Everything in this lesson turns on one legal phrase: passenger for hire. Get it wrong and you’re running an illegal charter. [+] A passenger for hire is a passenger for whom consideration is contributed as a condition of carriage. [+] Consideration means money, or any other economic benefit, given directly or indirectly. [+] But federal law carves out one thing: the voluntary sharing of a trip’s actual expenses. Friends splitting fuel and bait isn’t consideration. [+] And owners, crew, and true non-paying guests aren’t passengers for hire either. So here’s a test. Your neighbor says, take me and my buddies out Saturday, and we’ll each give you a hundred dollars. Is that a charter? [pause] Yes. The payment is a condition of going. [+] And it doesn’t matter what you call it. A donation, a club membership, a required fuel charge: if they have to pay to come, they’re passengers for hire. The key word is voluntary.

slides.heading: Uninspected vs inspected vessels

head: Vessel
Passengers for hire
Credential
rows: More than 6, up to the limit on its COI
Charterer hires the boat and supplies the captain
Strict rules; a common illegal-charter disguise

items: Strict rules; a common illegal disguise

slides.script: Here’s how the vessel categories fit together. [+] An uninspected passenger vessel carries no more than six passengers for hire, and the operator needs at least an OUPV. That’s your boat. [+] An inspected small passenger vessel carries more than six, up to the number on her Certificate of Inspection, and she needs a Master. [+] The third row is where captains get into trouble: the bareboat charter, also called a demise charter. In a real one, the charterer hires the boat and supplies his own captain, and the owner steps away completely. [pause] Why does that matter to you? Because fake bareboat charters are a classic way to dodge the six-passenger limit, and the Coast Guard fines operators for them regularly. If someone offers you a job running twelve people on an uninspected boat under a bareboat agreement, be very careful.

slides.heading: The boat’s paperwork

items: 5 net tons or more, passengers for hire between U.S. points: Coast Guard documentation with a coastwise endorsement
Florida: the right FWC charter fishing license covers your customers
Carry your credential, the boat’s papers and required placards aboard

slides.script: Your boat needs the right paperwork too, not just you. [+] A boat of five net tons or more, carrying passengers for hire between American points, must be documented by the Coast Guard with a coastwise endorsement. That endorsement also has rules about where the boat was built and who owns her. [+] Smaller boats are simply registered with the state. [+] In Florida there’s one more piece. A charter fishing operation needs the right saltwater charter license from the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. That license covers your customers, so they don’t each need their own. [+] And carry it all aboard: your credential, the boat’s papers, and the required placards. When the Coast Guard boards you, and one day they will, what do they ask for first? [pause] Your license and the boat’s documents. Have them where you can reach them in ten seconds.

slides.heading: Drugs and alcohol

items: Join a DOT drug testing program, usually through a consortium
Tests: pre-employment, random, post-casualty, reasonable cause
Commercial operators are intoxicated at 0.04% BAC
After a serious marine incident: alcohol test within 2 hours, drugs within 32 hours
Refusing a test can cost you your license
Alcohol test in 2 hours, drugs in 32

slides.script: One more thing comes with the license: drug and alcohol rules that are stricter than for any recreational boater. [+] As a commercial operator, you must be enrolled in a Department of Transportation drug testing program. Most owner-operators join a consortium that handles it. [+] The tests come before employment, at random, after a serious marine incident, and when there’s reasonable cause. [+] For alcohol, a commercial operator is intoxicated at zero point zero four percent. That’s half the recreational limit. [+] After a serious marine incident, the clock starts. Alcohol testing within two hours, drug testing within thirty-two hours. [+] And refusing a test can cost you your license. [pause] That’s lesson one. Six passengers, uninspected vessel, five years. If they have to pay to come, they’re passengers for hire. And zero point zero four, two hours, thirty-two hours. Next time: the safety gear the law requires on your boat.

slides.heading: Life jackets

items: An approved wearable life jacket for every person aboard
Passenger-carrying vessels: offshore (Type I or equivalent) life jackets
Readily accessible and in good condition
Plus a throwable device, usually a ring buoy

slides.script: Today is the equipment list: what the law says must be on your boat before a paying passenger steps aboard. We start where every boarding officer starts. Life jackets. [+] You need a Coast Guard approved wearable life jacket for every person aboard, in the right size. [+] And because you carry passengers for hire, they must be the offshore type, traditionally called Type one, with the most flotation. [+] Child sizes for every child. An adult jacket on a six-year-old doesn’t count, and it doesn’t work. [+] They must be readily accessible and in good condition. So are they legal if they’re still sealed in plastic under a locked seat? [pause] No. Readily accessible means a passenger can get one in seconds. Newer jackets carry performance-level labels instead of Types, and the older ones stay legal while they’re serviceable. [+] And you need a throwable device, usually a ring buoy, ready at hand.

slides.heading: Fire extinguishers
slides.script: Fire extinguishers go by boat length, and the exam loves the table. Assume no fixed system in the engine room. [+] Under twenty-six feet: one B-one. [+] Twenty-six to under forty feet: two B-ones, or one B-two. [+] Forty to sixty-five feet: three B-ones, or one B-two plus one B-one. See the pattern? One, two, three, and a B-two is worth two B-ones. [+] If you have an approved fixed system in the engine room, you need one fewer B-one. [+] And disposable extinguishers expire. Replace them twelve years after the date of manufacture. [pause] One labeling note. Newer extinguishers are marked five-B and twenty-B instead of B-one and B-two, and newer boats must carry those. Mount them where you can grab one without reaching over the thing that’s likely to be on fire.

slides.heading: Visual distress signals
slides.script: Visual distress signals are required on coastal waters: the ocean, the Gulf, and connected bays and sounds until they narrow to less than two miles wide. A boat sixteen feet or longer must carry signals for both day and night. Follow the table. [+] Red hand flares count for day and night. [+] So do red meteor and parachute flares. [+] Orange smoke is for day only. Why? [pause] You can’t see smoke in the dark. [+] The orange distress flag is also day only. [+] And the electric SOS light is night only. So three red flares cover you for both. Or you can pair a flag for day with an electric light for night, and carry no pyrotechnics at all. One date to remember: pyrotechnic signals expire forty-two months after manufacture. And never fire one except in a real emergency.

A boat sixteen feet or longer must carry signals for both day and night. Follow the table. Red hand flares count for day and night. So do red meteor and parachute flares. Orange smoke is for day only. Why? You can’t see smoke in the dark. The orange distress flag is also day only. And the electric SOS light is night only. So three red flares cover you for both. Or you can pair a flag for day with an electric light for night, and carry no pyrotechnics at all. One date to remember: pyrotechnic signals expire forty-two months after manufacture. And never fire one except in a real emergency.

slides.heading: Ventilation and flame arrestors

items: Gasoline engine spaces need natural and powered ventilation
Run the blower at least 4 minutes before starting
Gasoline inboards need a backfire flame arrestor
Diesels need ventilation for combustion air
On gasoline inboards. Keep it clean

slides.script: Now the equipment that keeps a gasoline boat from exploding. [+] Any gasoline engine in an enclosed space needs ventilation to carry vapor away: natural vents, plus a powered blower. [+] Run that blower for at least four minutes before you start the engine. Four minutes. Then use the best vapor detector aboard. What’s that? [pause] Your nose. Open the hatch and sniff the bilge. [+] Gasoline inboards and sterndrives must also have an approved backfire flame arrestor on the air intake. If the engine backfires, the arrestor stops the flame from reaching vapor in the compartment. [+] Keep it clean and firmly secured. An oily, loose arrestor doesn’t do its job. [+] Diesels are far less explosive, but their spaces still need ventilation, to feed the engine combustion air.

slides.heading: Everything else aboard

items: Oil and garbage placards on boats 26 ft and over
An approved marine sanitation device if there’s a toilet
A pre-departure safety briefing for passengers
Wise extras: EPIRB or PLB, VHF-DSC, first aid kit, high-water alarm

slides.script: A few more required items, and then the ones a professional carries anyway. [+] Navigation lights and sound-signaling equipment that meet the rules you just studied. [+] On boats twenty-six feet and over, the oil discharge placard and the garbage placard. [+] If there’s an installed toilet, a Coast Guard certified marine sanitation device. [+] And one thing that isn’t equipment at all: a safety briefing before every trip. Where the life jackets are, how to put one on, and what to do if something goes wrong. It takes two minutes at the dock. [+] Beyond the minimum, I’d carry a registered EPIRB or personal locator beacon, a VHF with DSC, a real first aid kit, and a high-water alarm. [pause] That’s lesson two. A Type one for everyone. Extinguishers: one, two, three by length. Flares expire at forty-two months. And four minutes on the blower. Next time: what to do when there’s a fire anyway.

slides.heading: How fire works
slides.script: Fire is the emergency every captain dreads. On the water there’s no fire department and nowhere to run. So today we learn how a fire works, because that tells you how to kill it. Look at the diagram. A fire needs three things: heat, fuel and oxygen. Plus a fourth, the chemical chain reaction that keeps it going. Take away any one, and the fire goes out. [pause] Cooling removes the heat. Smothering removes the oxygen. Shutting a valve removes the fuel. And dry chemical breaks the chain reaction. Fires are also sorted into classes by what’s burning. Class A is ordinary stuff that leaves ash: wood, cushions, line. Class B is flammable liquids that boil: gasoline and oil. That’s the most common boat fire. Class C is energized electrical equipment, think current. And Class D is combustible metals. A for ash, B for boil, C for current.

slides.heading: Extinguishing agents

head: Agent
Fire classes
Notes
rows: Most common on boats; messy and corrosive
Displaces oxygen; no residue; short range
Never a solid stream on fuel or electrical fires

slides.script: Each extinguishing agent suits certain fires, so match the agent to the class. [+] Dry chemical, rated A B C or B C, is the one on most boats. It works on nearly everything. The price is a corrosive powder all over your boat. [+] Carbon dioxide works on fuel and electrical fires by displacing the oxygen. It leaves no mess. But it has short range, and in a closed space it can suffocate you too. [+] Clean agents are what you’ll usually find in a fixed engine-room system. [+] Foam smothers fuel fires by floating on top of them. [+] And water. It’s excellent on Class A fires. But what happens if you hit burning gasoline with a solid stream of water? [pause] You spread it. And on live electrical gear, water conducts the current right back to you. So water is for Class A only.

slides.heading: Fighting a fire

items: Raise the alarm; life jackets on; passengers away from the fire
Position the boat so wind carries smoke and flames away
PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep
Keep an escape route behind you
Not out in seconds? Call Mayday and prepare to abandon
Aim at the base of the fire

slides.script: So a fire breaks out. What do you do, and in what order? [+] First, raise the alarm, get life jackets on everyone, and move your passengers away from the fire. People first. [+] Second, use the boat. Turn so the wind carries the smoke and flames away from your people. Usually that means putting the fire downwind. [+] Third, the extinguisher, and here’s the word to remember: PASS. Pull the pin. Aim at the base of the fire. Squeeze the handle. Sweep from side to side. Why the base? [pause] Because that’s where the fuel is. Spraying the flames does nothing. [+] Keep an escape route behind you. Never let the fire get between you and the way out. [+] And know when to quit. A small boat fire grows fast. If it isn’t out in seconds, call Mayday and prepare to abandon.

slides.heading: Engine compartment fires

items: Shut down engines, generator, blowers and fuel
Close vents and hatches to starve the fire
Don’t open the hatch: fresh air feeds it
Discharge the fixed system if it hasn’t fired
Wait at least 15 minutes before opening; extinguisher ready
Shut down engines, blowers and fuel

slides.script: The engine compartment fire is the most dangerous one on a small boat, and your instinct will be wrong. Your instinct says: open the hatch and look. Don’t. Here’s the drill. [+] Shut down the engines, the generator and the blowers, and close the fuel valves. [+] Close the vents and hatches to starve the fire of air. [+] And leave the hatch shut. What happens if you open it? [pause] A rush of fresh air, and the fire flares up in your face. [+] Discharge the fixed system, if it hasn’t gone off by itself. Many systems shut the engines down when they fire. [+] Then wait. At least fifteen minutes before you open that compartment, so it can cool and the fire can’t reignite. And when you do open it, have a portable extinguisher in your hand.

slides.heading: Electrical, galley and propane fires

items: Electrical: kill the power, then CO2 or dry chemical
Galley grease: smother with a lid or fire blanket, never water
Propane: close the tank valve; vapor sinks into the bilge
Fire blanket for clothing and small galley fires
Kill the power, then CO2 or dry chemical
Close the tank valve. Vapor sinks

slides.script: Three more kinds of fire, each with its own trick. [+] Electrical. Kill the power first, at the battery switch or the breaker. Then use carbon dioxide or dry chemical. With the power off, it’s often just a small Class A fire. [+] Galley grease. Smother it with a lid or a fire blanket, and turn off the heat. Never water. Water turns to steam and throws burning grease across the cabin. [+] Propane. Close the valve at the tank. And remember that propane is heavier than air, so a leak sinks into the bilge just like gasoline vapor. If you smell it, ventilate before you touch a single switch. [+] And keep a fire blanket handy. It’s the fastest way to put out burning clothing, too. [pause] That’s lesson three. Heat, fuel, oxygen, chain reaction. A for ash, B for boil, C for current. PASS, aimed at the base. And never open the engine hatch for fifteen minutes. Next time: how to keep the fire from starting at all.

lessons.title: Fueling, fire prevention and carbon monoxide

slides.heading: Gasoline vapor

items: Gasoline vapor is heavier than air and settles in the bilge
A small amount of vapor can cause a powerful explosion
Diesel is far less volatile, but still burns

els: Gasoline vapor is heavier than air
<path d='M80,110 H360 L328,290 Q220,336 112,290 Z' class='s-bg' style='stroke:var(--ink);stroke-width:2'/><ellipse cx='220' cy='284' rx='92' ry='24' fill='#e8762b' opacity='.55'/>

slides.script: Last time we fought the fire. Today we stop it from starting, and that begins with understanding one thing about gasoline. It isn’t the liquid that explodes. It’s the vapor. [+] Gasoline vapor is heavier than air. So where does it go? [pause] Down. It flows like water into the bilge and the low compartments, and it sits there, waiting for a spark from a switch, a pump or a starter. [+] And it doesn’t take much. A small amount of vapor can produce an explosion strong enough to destroy the boat. [+] Propane behaves the same way. It sinks too. [+] Diesel is far less volatile and much harder to light, which is one reason most commercial boats burn it. But once it’s lit, it still burns. Here’s the fact to carry with you: most boat explosions happen during fueling, or just after it.

slides.heading: Safe fueling, step by step

lines: Moor securely; passengers ashore if practical
Stop engines and motors; no smoking or open flame
Close hatches, ports and cabin doors
Keep the nozzle touching the fill pipe; don’t overfill
Wipe up spills, open up, run the blower 4+ minutes and sniff the bilge

items: Blower 4+ minutes, then sniff the bilge

slides.script: So fuel the same careful way, every single time. Here’s the routine. [+] Moor the boat securely, and if it’s practical, put your passengers ashore. [+] Stop the engines and every electric motor. No smoking, no open flame. [+] Close the hatches, ports and cabin doors. Why close up? [pause] Because the vapor is heavier than air, and you don’t want it flowing below. [+] Keep the nozzle touching the fill pipe the whole time, which prevents a static spark. And don’t fill to the brim. Fuel expands as it warms. [+] When you’re done, wipe up any spills, open everything back up, run the blower for at least four minutes, and sniff the bilge and the engine space before you turn the key. Close up to fuel. Open up to start.

slides.heading: Carbon monoxide

items: Builds near the stern, the swim platform and enclosed cabins
“Station wagon effect”: exhaust drawn aboard while underway
Symptoms mimic seasickness: headache, nausea, dizziness
Install CO alarms; no one on the swim platform with engines or generator running

els: <circle cx='130' cy='214' r='22' class='s-mut' opacity='.45'/><circle cx='106' cy='194' r='16' class='s-mut' opacity='.35'/><circle cx='150' cy='184' r='14' class='s-mut' opacity='.3'/>
and the swim platform, and gets drawn aboard

slides.script: Now a killer you can’t see or smell. Carbon monoxide. [+] It’s colorless, odorless, and deadly, and it’s in the exhaust of every engine and generator. [+] It collects near the stern, on and around the swim platform, and in enclosed cabins. [+] It can follow you, too. Underway, the airflow behind the boat can pull exhaust back aboard, especially with canvas up. That’s called the station wagon effect. [+] The early symptoms are headache, nausea and dizziness. What does that sound like on a boat? [pause] Seasickness. So when a passenger feels sick in the cabin with the generator running, don’t assume it’s the waves. Get them into fresh air. [+] Install and test carbon monoxide alarms in enclosed spaces. And nobody hangs on the swim platform with an engine or generator running. Ever.

slides.heading: Batteries and electrical systems

items: Charging batteries give off explosive hydrogen
Ventilate and secure batteries; cover the terminals
Use marine-rated wiring, breakers and fuses
Shore power: inspect cords and connectors
Electric shock drowning: never swim near docks with shore power
Never swim near docks with shore power

slides.script: Electrical systems start a great many boat fires, so a few rules. [+] Batteries give off hydrogen gas while they charge, and hydrogen is explosive. [+] So battery compartments need ventilation. The batteries must be secured so they can’t shift in a seaway, with the terminals covered. [+] Use marine-rated wiring, breakers and fuses. Household parts corrode and overheat. [+] Check your shore power cords and connectors. Brown or melted plastic means heat, and heat means a fire on its way. [+] And one danger most people have never heard of: electric shock drowning. Faulty wiring can put current into the water around a dock, especially in fresh or brackish water. A swimmer is paralyzed and drowns. So what’s the rule at any marina with shore power? [pause] Nobody swims there.

slides.heading: Good housekeeping

items: Keep bilges clean and free of oil and fuel
Inspect fuel lines, clamps, vents and tanks regularly
Store rags, paints and solvents properly
Smoking only where it’s safe, if at all
Prevention is far easier than firefighting

slides.script: Most boat fires are preventable, and prevention is plain housekeeping. [+] Keep the bilges clean, with no oil or fuel in them. A clean bilge also shows you a new leak right away. [+] Inspect the fuel lines, hose clamps, tank vents and tanks for chafe, corrosion and weeping. [+] Store oily rags, paints and solvents in proper containers. An oily rag wadded up in a locker can heat up and light all by itself. [+] Allow smoking only where it’s safe, if you allow it at all. [+] And remember that a few minutes of looking at the dock is far easier than fighting a fire offshore with six passengers aboard. [pause] That’s lesson four. Vapor sinks. Close up to fuel, open up to start, four minutes on the blower. Carbon monoxide looks like seasickness. And nobody swims near shore power. Next time: what keeps a boat upright.

slides.heading: G, B and M
slides.script: Why does a boat stay upright? And why, some days, doesn’t she? Today’s lesson answers both, and it comes down to three letters. Look at the diagram. G is the center of gravity. It’s where all the weight acts, and it pulls down. B is the center of buoyancy, the center of the underwater part of the hull, and it pushes up. Now heel the boat. What happens to B? [pause] It moves toward the low side, because more of the hull is underwater there. So now gravity pulls down in one place, and buoyancy pushes up in another, and together they twist the boat back upright. That’s the righting arm. The third letter is M, the metacenter: the point where the line straight up from B crosses the centerline. And the distance from G up to M is the metacentric height, G M. The bigger the G M, the more firmly she stands up.

slides.heading: What hurts stability

items: Free surface: sloshing liquid acts like raising G
Keep tanks full or empty, and bilges dry
Quick, snappy roll: stiff, large GM
Slow, lazy roll: tender, small GM

els: Free surface acts like raising G

<g transform='rotate(12 120 190)'><path d='M40,130 H200 L184,230 Q120,256 56,230 Z' class='s-bg' style='stroke:var(--ink);stroke-width:2'/><rect x='85' y='180' width='70' height='40' class='s-mag'/></g><g transform='rotate(12 320 190)'><path d='M240,130 H400 L384,230 Q320,256 256,230 Z' class='s-bg' style='stroke:var(--ink);stroke-width:2'/><rect x='285' y='180' width='70' height='40' fill='none' style='stroke:var(--ink);stroke-width:1.5'/><polygon points='285,220 355,220 355,190 285,208' class='s-mag'/></g>
Liquid runs to the low side
Keep tanks full or empty, and bilges dry

slides.script: So what makes G M smaller? Anything that raises G. [+] Add weight high up, and G goes up. Passengers in a tower. Gear stacked on the cabin top. [+] The second enemy is sneakier: free surface. Liquid sloshing in a half-full tank runs to the low side when you heel, and it pushes you over further. It acts just like raising G. [+] So keep tanks either full or empty when you can, and keep the bilges dry. [+] Here’s the useful part. You can feel your stability through your feet. A quick, snappy roll means a stiff boat, with a large G M. [+] A slow, lazy roll, where she leans over and takes her time coming back, means a tender boat, with a small G M. And if your boat rolls lazier this afternoon than she did this morning, what’s that telling you? [pause] Something changed. Look for water.

slides.heading: Passengers and loading

items: Passengers rushing to one rail can capsize a small boat
Keep heavy loads low and centered
Respect the capacity plate on small boats
Fuel, ice and fish change your loading during the day
Water on deck acts like free surface

b: Keep heavy loads low. Respect the capacity plate

slides.script: On a charter, the biggest stability problem isn’t fuel or ice. It’s people. [+] Picture it. Somebody hooks a big kingfish on the port side, and all six passengers rush to the port rail to watch. On a small boat, that alone can swamp or capsize her. So what do you say before lines go in the water? [pause] Stay spread out. One or two at the rail, the rest stay put. [+] Keep heavy things, coolers, ice and gear, low and near the centerline. [+] On small boats, respect the capacity plate. [+] And remember that your loading changes all day. You burn off fuel, the ice melts, and the fish box fills up. The boat you bring home isn’t the boat you took out. [+] Finally, water trapped on deck is free surface, right where you can least afford it: up high.

slides.heading: Words to know

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Temporary lean from wind, waves or a turn
Steady lean from off-center weight or flooding
Fore-and-aft balance: down by the bow or stern
Height from the waterline to the deck edge

slides.script: Five words you need for the exam, and for talking to the Coast Guard on the radio. [+] Heel is a temporary lean, from wind, waves or a turn. [+] List is a steady lean, caused by weight off-center, or by flooding. So if your boat develops a list and nobody moved anything, what do you check? [pause] The bilge. An unexplained list means water is getting in. [+] Trim is the fore-and-aft balance. We say down by the bow or down by the stern. [+] Freeboard is the height from the waterline up to the deck edge. [+] And reserve buoyancy is the watertight volume above the waterline. It’s your margin, the thing that keeps you afloat as you take on load or water. Here’s how I keep the first two apart. Heel heals itself. A list lasts.
slides.spoken: Five words you need for the exam, and for talking to the Coast Guard on the radio. Heel is a temporary lean, from wind, waves or a turn. List is a steady lean, caused by weight off-center, or by flooding. So if your boat develops a list and nobody moved anything, what do you check? The bilge. An unexplained list means water is getting in. Trim is the fore-and-aft balance. We say down by the bow or down by the stern. Freeboard is the height from the waterline up to the deck edge. And reserve buoyancy is the watertight volume above the waterline. It’s your margin, the thing that keeps you afloat as you take on load or water. Here’s how I keep the first two apart. Heel heals itself. A list lasts.

slides.heading: How boats capsize

items: Free surface and water in the boat
Down-flooding through open hatches or a low transom
Free surface, water in the boat

slides.script: So how do small boats actually capsize? Almost never from one cause. It’s a stack of them. [+] Too much weight, or weight carried too high. [+] Free surface, and water already in the boat. [+] A sharp turn at speed. [+] A following sea that slews her sideways into a broach. [+] And down-flooding: water pouring in through an open hatch, or over a low transom. What’s the common thread? [pause] The boat was already near her limit before the last wave arrived. So keep weight low. Keep water out. Slow down in rough water. And keep your bow or your stern, never your beam, toward breaking seas. That’s lesson five. G pulls down, B pushes up, and G M is your stability. Snappy is stiff, lazy is tender. Heel heals, a list lasts. Next time: hulls, and keeping the water on the outside.

slides.heading: Hull types

items: Displacement hulls push through the water; speed limited by length
Planing hulls rise onto the surface at speed
Deep-V: smoother in chop; flat bottom: stable at rest, pounds in waves

els: Planing: rises onto the surface at speed

slides.script: Hull shape determines how a boat behaves. A displacement hull pushes through the water, and its top speed, called hull speed, is limited by its waterline length. A planing hull rises up and skims on the surface once it has enough power and speed, which is how most charter boats travel. Semi-displacement hulls fall in between. A deep-V bottom cuts through chop and gives a smoother ride, while a flat bottom is very stable at rest and in shallow water but pounds hard in waves.

slides.heading: Keeping the water out

items: Close hatches, ports and doors in rough water
Keep scuppers and freeing ports clear
Inspect seacocks, hoses and double clamps below the waterline
Down-flooding through open hatches sinks boats fast

slides.script: Watertight integrity means keeping water out of the hull. In rough water, close hatches, ports and doors. Scuppers and freeing ports must be kept clear so water on deck drains overboard instead of building up. Below the waterline, inspect every seacock, hose and fitting, and use double stainless hose clamps. A failed hose or through-hull fitting is one of the most common reasons boats sink at the dock. Underway, water pouring through an open hatch in heavy seas, called down-flooding, can sink a boat in minutes.

slides.heading: Bilge pumps and alarms

items: Automatic electric pumps with float switches
A high-water alarm you can hear at the helm
Pump capacity drops with lift and hose length
Loud enough to hear at the helm

slides.script: Every boat needs reliable bilge pumping. Automatic electric pumps with float switches handle small leaks and rainwater, and a high-water alarm audible at the helm warns you when something is wrong. Carry a manual pump as a backup in case of electrical failure. Remember that a pump’s rated capacity drops sharply with the height it lifts water and the length of its hose, so real-world output is much less than the label. Most importantly, know where every through-hull fitting on your boat is, so you can find a leak fast.

slides.heading: Responding to flooding

lines: Find the source: through-hulls, hoses, shaft seal, hull damage
Stop or slow it: close seacocks, drive soft wood plugs, stuff cushions or rags
Pump: every pump you have, plus buckets
Call for help early: Pan-pan, or Mayday if sinking
Life jackets on everyone; head for shallow water if close

slides.script: If you discover flooding, act in order. First, find the source: check through-hulls, hoses, the shaft seal and the hull itself. Second, stop or slow the leak: close the seacock, drive a soft wood plug into a failed fitting, or stuff cushions and rags into a hole. Tie a plug next to every through-hull so it’s there when you need it. Third, pump with everything you have. Fourth, call for help early, with a pan-pan, or a Mayday if you’re sinking. Get life jackets on everyone, and if the leak is winning, head for shallow water.

slides.heading: Following seas

items: Broach: a following sea slews the boat sideways
Pitchpole: the bow digs in and the stern flips over
Run inlets on the back of a wave, not down its face
Raise trim tabs to keep the bow up

els: Broaching and pitchpoling start on the face

slides.script: Following seas are especially dangerous for small powerboats. A broach happens when a wave from astern lifts the stern and slews the boat sideways, where the next wave can roll it. In extreme cases a boat can pitchpole, with the bow burying and the stern flipping over the top. When running before big seas or entering an inlet, ride on the back of a wave, matching its speed, rather than surfing down its face. Raise the trim tabs to keep the bow up, and be ready with the throttle.

slides.heading: Propeller walk
slides.script: A propeller does more than push. Its blades also push the stern sideways, called propeller walk or prop walk. On a single-screw boat with a right-hand propeller, which turns clockwise when viewed from astern going ahead, the stern kicks slightly to starboard going ahead and walks strongly to port going astern. That’s why many single-screw captains prefer to dock port side to: a burst of reverse to stop the boat also pulls the stern in toward the dock. Learn which way your boat walks before you need it.

slides.heading: How boats steer

items: Inboards steer by water flowing over the rudder
Little flow means little steering, especially astern
A short burst of power gives steering without much speed
Going ahead, a boat pivots about a third of its length from the bow
Outboards and sterndrives steer by aiming thrust

slides.script: An inboard boat steers by water flowing past the rudder, mostly prop wash. At low speed, especially in reverse, there’s little flow, and steering is poor. A short burst of power with the rudder over gives steering without building much speed. Going ahead, a boat pivots about a point roughly a third of its length back from the bow, so the stern swings wide in a turn, which matters when you’re turning near a dock or another boat. Outboards and sterndrives steer by aiming the propeller’s thrust, so they respond well even at low speed.

slides.heading: Twin screws

items: Outboard-turning props cancel each other’s walk
One ahead, one astern: the boat spins in place
At low speed, steer with the engines; rudders centered
Use small bursts and neutral often

slides.script: Most twin-screw boats have counter-rotating propellers that cancel each other’s walk. Twins give tremendous control at low speed. With one engine ahead and the other astern, the boat spins in place. Put the starboard engine ahead and the port engine astern to turn to port, and the reverse to turn to starboard. Around docks, center the rudders and steer with the engines alone, using short bursts of power and plenty of neutral rather than holding the shifters in gear.

slides.heading: Docking principles

items: Approach slowly: never faster than you’re willing to hit the dock
Approach into the stronger of wind or current
Have fenders and lines rigged before you arrive
Use spring lines to hold or pivot the boat
Brief crew: fend off with fenders or a boat hook, never hands or feet

els: Approach slowly, into the wind or current
Never faster than you’re willing to hit the dock

slides.script: Good docking is about planning. Approach slowly, never faster than you’re willing to hit the dock. Figure out whether wind or current is stronger, and approach into it, which gives you control and lets you stop easily. Have fenders and lines rigged before you arrive, and brief your crew or mate on which line goes where. A spring line can hold the boat against the dock while others are made fast, or pivot it in or out. Never let anyone fend off with their hands or feet, since crushing injuries between boat and dock are common.

slides.heading: Wind and current at the dock

items: Wind blowing onto the dock: stop alongside and let it push you in
Wind blowing off the dock: steeper approach; get a bow line or spring on fast
Current from ahead: easiest; current from astern: approach with care
Leaving: spring out the stern or bow against a line

a: Stop alongside and let it push you in
b: Steeper approach. Get a bow line or spring on fast

slides.script: Wind and current change everything. With the wind blowing onto the dock, stop parallel a few feet off and let the wind set you gently alongside. With the wind blowing off the dock, approach at a steeper angle, get a bow line or spring line on quickly, and use it to pull the boat in. A current from ahead is easiest to dock against, while a current from astern pushes you faster than you think, so turn around if you can. To leave, motor gently ahead against a bow spring with the wheel turned toward the dock to swing the stern out, then back away.

slides.heading: Line materials

head: Material
Stretch
Floats?
Used for
rows: Ring buoy lines, ski ropes; weakens in sun

slides.script: Choose line by what it needs to do. Nylon is strong and stretchy, so it absorbs shock loads, which makes it ideal for anchor rodes, dock lines and towlines. Polyester, often sold as Dacron, is strong with little stretch, used for halyards and sheets. Polypropylene floats, which makes it useful for ring buoy lines and ski ropes, but it’s weaker and breaks down in sunlight. Spectra and Dyneema are extremely strong, low-stretch, floating fibers used in specialty lines.

slides.heading: Construction and care

items: Double braid: strong and smooth, easy on hands and winches
Protect against chafe with chafe gear
Rinse out salt; store out of the sun
A knot weakens a line far more than a splice

b: Strong and smooth, easy on hands and winches

slides.script: Lines come in different constructions. Three-strand twisted line is easy to splice and stretches well, which suits anchor rodes. Double-braid line is strong and smooth, easier on hands and winches. Chafe is the biggest enemy of line, so protect lines where they pass through chocks or over edges with chafe gear. Rinse out salt and store lines out of the sun. Remember that tying a knot in a line can reduce its strength by a third or more, while a good splice keeps most of it.

slides.heading: Dock lines
slides.script: A boat at a dock is usually held by four or more lines. The bow line runs forward from the bow, and the stern line runs aft from the stern, both holding the boat in to the dock. Spring lines control fore-and-aft movement. The bow spring runs from near the bow aft to the dock and stops the boat surging forward, while the stern spring runs from near the stern forward and stops it moving back. A breast line runs straight across to hold the boat close. Leave slack for the tide, or the boat can hang from its lines as the water falls.

slides.heading: Knots every captain knows

head: Knot
Use
rows: A fixed loop that won’t slip and unties easily
Securing a line to a cleat
A quick hitch to a piling or rail; can slip
Round turn and two half hitches
Secure attachment to a ring or post under load
Joining two lines, even of different sizes
A stopper knot at the end of a line
Taking the strain off another line

slides.script: A captain should be able to tie these knots without thinking. The bowline makes a fixed loop that won’t slip and unties easily even after a heavy load. The cleat hitch secures a line to a cleat. The clove hitch is a quick hitch around a piling or rail, but it can slip, so back it up. A round turn and two half hitches secures a line to a ring or post under load. The sheet bend joins two lines, even of different sizes. The figure-eight is a stopper knot. And the rolling hitch grips another line to take the strain off it. Practice them until your hands know them.

slides.heading: Line safety

items: Snap-back: a parting line can kill
Stay out of the path of a line under load
Never stand in a bight or loop of line
Use the right size line for the load
Inspect for chafe, stiffness and sun damage

els: <rect x='40' y='186' width='24' height='28' rx='4' class='s-ink'/>
Stay out of the line of pull
Never stand in a bight or loop of line

slides.script: Lines under load store tremendous energy, especially stretchy nylon. If a loaded line parts, it can snap back with enough force to kill, so keep yourself and your passengers out of the path of any line under strain, such as during towing or when a boat surges against its dock lines. Never stand inside a bight, or loop, of line, where it could tighten around a leg. Use lines sized for the load, and inspect them for chafe, stiffness and sun damage, replacing them before they fail.

slides.heading: Types of anchors
slides.script: Choose an anchor for the bottom you’ll use. A fluke anchor, often called a Danforth, is light, stows flat, and holds very well in sand and mud, which makes it the most common anchor on Florida fishing boats, but it can struggle in grass and rock. A plow or claw anchor holds in most bottoms and resets itself if the wind shifts. A mushroom anchor works by suction in soft mud and is used for permanent moorings. A grapnel hooks into rocks and wrecks and is popular for fishing structure on small boats, but it can foul, so rig it to break free.

slides.heading: Rode and scope
slides.script: The rode is everything between the anchor and the boat. Most small boats use a length of chain at the anchor, which keeps the pull low along the bottom and resists chafe on rocks and shells, then nylon line, which stretches to absorb shock. Scope is the ratio of rode let out to the distance from your bow to the bottom: the water depth plus the height of the bow above the water. Five to one is the minimum and seven to one is preferred, with more in heavy weather. In fifteen feet of water with a bow three feet high, seven to one means eighteen times seven, or one hundred twenty-six feet.

slides.heading: Setting the anchor

lines: Choose a spot with good bottom, shelter and room to swing
Head slowly into the wind or current and stop
Lower the anchor to the bottom; never throw it
Drift or back slowly while paying out scope
Set it with gentle reverse; take bearings or set a GPS anchor alarm

items: Head into wind or current, and stop

slides.script: To anchor, choose a spot with good holding bottom, shelter from the expected wind, and room to swing a full circle without hitting anything. Approach slowly into the wind or current and stop over the spot. Lower the anchor to the bottom, never throw it, since a thrown anchor tangles its own rode. Let the boat drift or back slowly downwind as you pay out scope. Snub the line to let the anchor bite, then set it firmly with gentle reverse. Finally, take bearings on two landmarks or set a GPS anchor alarm, so you’ll know if you start to drag.

slides.heading: Dragging and fouled anchors

items: Signs of dragging: bearings change, the rode jerks, the boat lies differently
Let out more scope, or pick up and re-anchor
Always anchor from the bow, never the stern
A trip line on the crown frees a fouled anchor
Keep an anchor watch in changing weather

slides.script: Watch for signs of dragging: your bearings or GPS position keep changing, the rode jerks or vibrates, or the boat lies at a different angle to the wind than nearby boats. Let out more scope, or pick up and re-anchor. Always anchor from the bow, never the stern. A boat anchored by the stern presents its low transom to the waves and can be swamped in minutes. If your anchor fouls under a rock or ledge, a trip line tied to the anchor’s crown lets you pull it out backward. And keep an anchor watch whenever the weather is changing.

slides.heading: Where not to anchor

items: Not in channels, cable areas or restricted areas
Show an anchor light at night and a ball by day
Florida Keys sanctuary: never on coral; use mooring buoys
Leave swing room for other boats
Not in channels or cable areas
Ball by day, anchor light at night
Never on coral: use mooring buoys

slides.script: Don’t anchor in navigation channels, cable and pipeline areas, or restricted areas, and avoid anchoring where you’ll block other traffic. At night show your anchor light, and by day a black ball, as Rule thirty requires. In the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, anchoring on coral is prohibited, so use the mooring buoys provided at popular reefs. Avoid anchoring in seagrass where you can, and leave enough room for other boats to swing without hitting you when the wind or current changes.

lessons.title: Heavy weather, inlets, towing and groundings

slides.heading: Preparing for heavy weather

items: Check the forecast; when in doubt, don’t go
Life jackets on everyone in rough conditions
Secure loose gear and close hatches
Slow down; take head seas at a slight angle
Keep passengers seated, low and centered

els: Take head seas at a slight angle
Slow down. Everyone seated, low and centered

slides.script: The best heavy weather tactic is not to be out in it. Check the forecast, and when in doubt, don’t go. If weather catches you, have everyone put on life jackets, secure loose gear, and close hatches and doors. Slow down. Pounding into head seas at speed injures passengers and damages boats, so take them at a slight angle off the bow at a speed that lets the boat ride over each wave. Keep passengers seated low and near the center of the boat, where the motion is least.

slides.heading: Inlets

items: Inlets are where charter boats most often get into trouble
Strong ebb against an onshore wind builds breaking seas
Watch several sets before you commit
Running in: ride the back of a wave; don’t surf down the face
Wait for a better tide if you need to

slides.script: Florida’s inlets are where many charter boats get into trouble. When a strong ebb current runs out against an onshore wind or swell, waves stack up and break in the entrance. Before running an inlet, stand off and watch several sets of waves to learn their pattern. When running in, position the boat on the back of a wave and match its speed, staying there rather than surfing down its face, where you can broach. If conditions look bad, wait for slack water or the flood, or use another inlet. Coming home a little late beats not coming home.

slides.heading: Towing a disabled boat
slides.script: Sometimes you’ll be asked to tow another boat. Attach the towline to strong points with a bridle that spreads the load between two cleats, not to a single small cleat or a rail. Use a long towline with a sag in it, which absorbs shock like a spring, and keep the speed low, well below planing. Keep everyone clear of the towline, since a parting line can snap back with deadly force, and keep a knife ready to cut free in an emergency. In serious conditions, it’s often wiser to stand by and call a professional towing service or the Coast Guard.

Use a long towline with a sag in it, which absorbs shock like a spring, and keep the speed low, well below planing. Keep everyone clear of the towline, since a parting line can snap back with deadly force, and keep a knife ready to cut free in an emergency. In serious conditions, it’s often wiser to stand by and call a professional towing service or the Coast Guard.

slides.heading: Running aground

lines: Stop the engine; check everyone for injuries
Check for leaks and damage before trying to move
Don’t back hard: you can suck sand into the cooling system or open a hole
Shift weight, kedge off with an anchor, or wait for the rising tide
An unintended grounding is a reportable marine casualty

items: Stop the engine. Check for injuries
Shift weight, kedge off, or wait for the tide

slides.script: If you run aground, stop the engine and check everyone for injuries. Before trying to move, check the bilge and hull for leaks, because backing a holed boat off a shoal can sink it in deeper water. Don’t just back hard: you can pull sand and mud into the engine’s cooling system and make things worse. Try shifting weight, carrying an anchor out to deeper water and pulling yourself off, which is called kedging, or simply waiting for the rising tide. Remember that an unintended grounding of a commercial vessel is a reportable marine casualty.

slides.heading: After a collision

items: Check passengers and crew for injuries first
Assess damage and flooding on your boat
Render assistance to the other vessel’s people
Exchange names, vessel information and registration

slides.script: After a collision, your first concern is people: check your passengers and crew for injuries. Next, check your own boat for damage and flooding. Federal law requires the operator of a vessel involved in a collision to render assistance to people affected, as far as possible without serious danger to their own vessel, and to give their name, address and vessel identification. Never leave the scene without doing so. Then report the collision as required, to the Coast Guard for a commercial marine casualty.

slides.heading: The first seconds

items: Shout “Man overboard!” and point, and keep pointing
Turn toward the side they fell from to swing the props away
Assign one spotter who never looks away
Turn toward the side they fell from

slides.script: When someone falls overboard, the first seconds matter most. Shout man overboard, and point at the person, and keep pointing. Throw flotation immediately, a ring buoy, cushion, anything that floats, which also marks the spot. Press the man overboard button on your GPS. Turn the boat toward the side the person fell from, which swings the stern and propellers away from them. Assign one person whose only job is to keep their eyes and arm on the person in the water, because a head in waves disappears from sight within seconds.

slides.heading: The Williamson turn
slides.script: Several recovery turns exist. The Williamson turn brings you back down your own track, which makes it the best choice at night or when you’ve lost sight of the person. Put the rudder hard over toward the side the person fell from. When you’re about sixty degrees off your original course, shift the rudder hard over the other way. Steady up on the reciprocal of your original course, and you’ll be running back down your track toward the person. When the person is in sight and close, a quicker single turn, like the Anderson turn, brings you back faster.

slides.heading: Getting them back aboard

items: Approach slowly, heading into the wind or sea
Put the engine in neutral close to the person
Recover over the side, never near the propeller
Use a ladder, sling or parbuckle
Treat for hypothermia and shock; get medical help

els: <circle cx='254' cy='176' r='9' fill='#e8762b'/><path d='M240,190 q14,-8 28,0' stroke='#e8762b' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/>
Approach slowly, into the wind or sea
Neutral when close. Recover over the side,

slides.script: Approach the person slowly, ideally heading into the wind or sea so you can stop alongside under control. Shift to neutral well before you reach them, and keep the propeller away. Never approach stern first. Bring them aboard over the side, not at the stern near the propeller, using a boarding ladder, a sling, or a parbuckle made from a line or net. A tired or cold person can’t climb, so plan to lift them. Once aboard, treat for hypothermia and shock, and get medical help.

slides.heading: Surviving in the water

items: A life jacket is the difference between living and drowning
1-10-1: 1 minute of cold shock, 10 of useful movement, 1 hour to unconsciousness
HELP: knees to chest, arms crossed, if alone
Stay with the boat if it floats; don’t swim for distant shore
The difference between living and drowning

slides.script: In the water, a life jacket is the difference between surviving and drowning. Cold water shock makes people gasp and inhale water in the first minute, which is why so many drownings happen to people who could swim. A useful guide is one, ten, one: about one minute of cold shock, ten minutes of meaningful movement before muscles fail, and about an hour before hypothermia causes unconsciousness in cold water. Florida’s water is warmer, which buys more time, but not unlimited time. Alone, hold the HELP position with knees to chest and arms crossed. In a group, huddle together. Stay with the boat if it floats, and don’t try to swim for distant shore.

slides.heading: Abandoning ship

items: Only when the boat is clearly lost
First: Mayday, DSC alert and EPIRB
Life jackets on; take a grab bag with radio, beacon and water
Step up into a life raft, not down
Stay together and near the boat’s last position
Life jackets on; take the grab bag
Step UP into the life raft

slides.script: Abandon the boat only when it’s clearly lost, because even a swamped boat is easier for rescuers to find than people in the water. Before leaving, send a Mayday by voice and DSC, and activate the EPIRB. Make sure everyone has a life jacket on, and grab a ditch bag with a handheld radio, personal locator beacon, flares, water and medications. The old saying is to step up into a life raft, meaning leave only when the boat is sinking out from under you. Stay together, and stay near the boat’s last known position, where searchers will start looking.

slides.heading: Mayday, pan-pan, securité

lines: Channel 16, or the DSC distress button first
“Mayday, Mayday, Mayday”
“This is Reel Time, Reel Time, Reel Time”
Position, nature of distress, help needed
Number aboard, boat description, then listen

fig.cap: Channel 16, or the red DSC button first
fig.sub: Then: who you are, where you are, what’s wrong, how many aboard

slides.script: There are three levels of urgent call. Mayday means grave and imminent danger to life or the vessel, such as sinking, fire or a man overboard. Pan-pan means an urgent situation without immediate danger to life, like a disabled engine drifting offshore. Securité is a safety message, such as a navigation hazard. A Mayday is sent on VHF channel sixteen, following the script on screen: Mayday three times, your boat’s name three times, your position, the problem, the help you need, the number aboard and a description of the boat. Then release the button and listen.

slides.heading: DSC and beacons

items: DSC red button: sends MMSI and position on channel 70
Then follow up by voice on channel 16
EPIRB: 406 MHz, registered with NOAA; float-free or manual
PLB: a personal beacon worn by a person
Sends MMSI and position on channel 70

slides.script: A VHF radio with digital selective calling has a red distress button. Pressing it sends an automatic alert with your MMSI number and GPS position on channel seventy, which the Coast Guard and nearby DSC radios receive. Then follow up by voice on channel sixteen. An EPIRB sends a distress signal on four hundred six megahertz to satellites, which relay your identity and position to rescuers. It must be registered with NOAA. A personal locator beacon does the same for an individual. Keep beacon registrations, batteries and hydrostatic releases current.

slides.heading: Radio procedures

items: Use the phonetic alphabet: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie…
“Over” invites a reply; “Out” ends the call
Radio checks on a working channel or automated service, not 16
Call on 16 or 9, then move to a working channel
A false distress call is a federal crime
Over invites a reply. Out ends the call

slides.script: Good radio habits matter. Use the phonetic alphabet to spell names and numbers: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta and so on. Say over when you want a reply, and out when the conversation is finished. Do radio checks on a working channel or an automated radio-check service, never on channel sixteen. Make initial calls on sixteen or nine, then switch to a working channel to talk. And never make a false distress call. It’s a federal crime that can bring fines, prison and the cost of the search.

slides.heading: Working with rescuers

items: Secure loose gear and canvas before a helicopter arrives
Let the basket or hook touch the water or deck first to discharge static
Never tie the hoist cable to the boat
Keep life jackets on and a light or flare ready

Let the basket touch down first

slides.script: When rescuers arrive, follow their instructions exactly. They may ask you to hold a certain course and speed. Before a helicopter arrives, secure loose gear, canvas and antennas that its rotor wash could blow around. Let the rescue basket or hook touch the water or deck before anyone touches it, because it carries a powerful static charge. Never tie the hoist cable to your boat. Keep everyone in life jackets, and have a light, flare or signal mirror ready to help them find you.

slides.heading: Float plans

items: Leave a float plan with a responsible person ashore
Who’s aboard, the boat, your route and return time
What to do, and whom to call, if you’re overdue
Update it if plans change; cancel it when you return
Whom to call if you’re overdue

slides.script: A float plan tells someone ashore where you’re going and when you’ll be back, so that if you don’t return, a search starts quickly and in the right place. Include who’s aboard, a description of the boat, your planned route, and your expected return time, plus instructions on when to call the Coast Guard. Leave it with a responsible person, such as your office, marina or a family member. Update it if your plans change, and cancel it when you get back.

slides.heading: Priorities

items: Make sure the scene is safe, then check responsiveness and breathing
Call for help early: VHF 16 or 911
CPR: hard and fast, 100 to 120 compressions a minute, about 2 inches deep
Use an AED if you carry one
Keep in-person CPR and first aid training current

fig.cap: Compressions a minute: hard, fast, about 2 inches deep
fig.sub: Scene safe, check breathing, call for help early

slides.script: Offshore, help may be an hour or more away, so first aid skills matter. Start by making sure the scene is safe for you. Then check whether the person responds and is breathing normally. Call for help early, on VHF channel sixteen or by phone, because the Coast Guard can arrange medical advice and evacuation. If the person isn’t breathing normally, start CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, one hundred to one hundred twenty compressions a minute, about two inches deep. Use an AED if you have one. Your license requires current CPR and first aid training, so keep it fresh.

slides.heading: Bleeding and shock

items: Tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding; note the time
Shock: pale, cold, clammy, fast pulse
Lay them flat, keep them warm, raise the legs if uninjured
Nothing to eat or drink if seriously hurt
Shock: lay flat, keep warm, raise the legs

slides.script: For serious bleeding, apply firm, direct pressure on the wound with a dressing and keep pressing. For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that pressure won’t control, apply a tourniquet high on the limb, tighten it until the bleeding stops, and note the time. Watch for shock, a life-threatening drop in circulation, with pale, cold, clammy skin and a fast, weak pulse. Lay the person flat, keep them warm, and raise their legs if they aren’t injured. Don’t give anything to eat or drink to someone seriously hurt.

slides.heading: Heat and cold

head: Condition
Signs
Treatment
rows: Pale, cool, sweaty skin; weak; nauseous
Emergency: cool aggressively, call for help
Remove wet clothes, insulate, warm the core gently
Prevent with shade, sunscreen and water

items: Cool, sweaty skin: shade, fluids, rest

slides.script: Florida charters see a lot of heat illness. Heat exhaustion causes pale, cool, sweaty skin, weakness and nausea. Get the person into shade, cool them, give fluids and let them rest. Heat stroke is a true emergency, with hot skin, confusion or collapse. Cool them aggressively with water and fanning, and call for help immediately. Hypothermia can happen even in Florida after time in the water. Remove wet clothing, insulate the person, and warm the core gently. Don’t rub their arms and legs, and don’t give alcohol. Prevent sunburn and dehydration with shade, sunscreen and plenty of water.

slides.heading: Marine injuries

items: Fish hooks: leave one in near the eye or a joint and seek care
Stingray, catfish and lionfish spines: soak in water as hot as tolerable
Jellyfish: rinse with seawater, not fresh water
Cuts from fish, shells and coral: clean well; watch for Vibrio infection
Seasickness: fresh air, watch the horizon, stay on deck
Soak in water as hot as tolerable
Rinse with seawater, not fresh water

slides.script: Fishing charters bring their own injuries. A fish hook in or near the eye, or deep in a joint, should be left in place, secured, and treated ashore. Venomous spines from stingrays, catfish and lionfish cause intense pain, and soaking the wound in water as hot as the person can tolerate without burning breaks down the venom. Rinse jellyfish stings with seawater, not fresh water, which can trigger more stinging cells. Clean cuts from fish, shells and coral well, because warm Florida waters carry Vibrio bacteria, which can cause serious infection, especially in people with liver disease or weak immune systems. For seasickness, keep the person on deck in fresh air, looking at the horizon.

slides.heading: Burns, fractures and head injuries

items: Burns: cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes; cover loosely
Fractures: immobilize as found; check circulation beyond the injury
Head, neck or back injury: don’t move them unless necessary
Eyes: don’t rub; flush with clean water
Record what happened and what you did
Don’t move them unless you must
Don’t rub. Flush with clean water

slides.script: For burns, cool the area under cool running water for ten to twenty minutes, then cover it loosely with a clean dressing. Don’t use ice, butter or ointments. For a suspected fracture, immobilize the limb in the position you found it, and check circulation beyond the injury. If you suspect a head, neck or back injury, such as from a fall in rough seas, keep the person still and don’t move them unless they’re in danger. For something in the eye, don’t rub it; flush with clean water. And always write down what happened and what you did, both for the medical team and for your casualty report.

slides.heading: Oil

items: No discharge that causes a sheen or sludge
Report every spill to the National Response Center
Never use soap or dispersants on a spill
Carry absorbent pads; no oily bilge water overboard

fig.cap: National Response Center: report every spill
fig.sub: No discharge that causes a sheen. Never use soap on a spill

slides.script: The Clean Water Act prohibits discharging oil or oily waste in any amount that causes a film or sheen on the water or sludge below the surface. If a spill happens, report it right away to the National Response Center at one, eight hundred, four two four, eight eight zero two. Never use dish soap or chemical dispersants to make a sheen disappear. That just sinks the oil, and it’s a violation itself. Carry absorbent pads to soak up spills and oil in the bilge, and never pump oily bilge water overboard.

slides.heading: Placards and plans

head: Requirement
Applies to
rows: Boats 26 ft and over with machinery spaces
MARPOL Annex V garbage placard (4 × 9 in)
Ocean-going boats 40 ft and over with a galley and berthing

slides.script: Boats twenty-six feet and over must post an oil discharge placard, at least five by eight inches, in the machinery space or at the bilge pump control station, warning that discharging oil is prohibited. They must also post a garbage placard, at least four by nine inches, summarizing the garbage discharge rules where crew and passengers can read it. Ocean-going boats forty feet and over that have a galley and berthing must also have a written waste management plan describing how garbage is collected, stored and disposed of, and who’s responsible.

slides.heading: Garbage: MARPOL Annex V

head: Garbage
Rule
rows: Plastics, including fishing line and nets
Only 3 nm or more from land
Only 12 nm or more from land
Paper, glass, metal and most other garbage

slides.script: Garbage rules come from MARPOL Annex five. Plastics, including monofilament fishing line, nets and bags, may never be discharged anywhere. Food waste may be discharged only well offshore: three nautical miles or more if it’s ground up, and twelve nautical miles or more if it isn’t. Most other garbage, like paper, glass and metal, may not be thrown overboard at all and must be brought ashore. Inside three miles and on inland waters, nothing goes overboard. The simplest rule for a charter boat: bring everything back to the dock.

slides.heading: Sewage and marine sanitation devices

head: Type
How it works
Discharge
rows: Treated effluent, outside no-discharge zones; boats 65 ft and under
Pump out ashore, or untreated only beyond 3 nm
No sewage at all, treated or not

slides.script: A boat with an installed toilet must have a Coast Guard certified marine sanitation device. Type one and Type two devices treat sewage so treated effluent can be discharged, except in no-discharge zones. Type one is limited to boats sixty-five feet and under. A Type three device is a holding tank, emptied at a pump-out station, or discharged untreated only more than three miles offshore. In no-discharge zones, including the whole Florida Keys sanctuary, no sewage at all may be discharged, treated or not, and Y-valves must be secured closed.

slides.heading: Protecting Florida’s waters

items: Manatee zones: obey idle-speed and slow-speed signs
Seagrass: don’t prop-scar; it’s illegal in many areas
Florida Keys sanctuary rules on anchoring, fishing and discharges
Recycle fishing line: it kills birds, turtles and dolphins
Report spills, injured wildlife and violations: FWC 888-404-3922
Manatee zones: idle or slow speed

slides.script: Florida’s waters are your business, so protect them. Obey manatee zone speed signs, and keep a lookout for manatees and sea turtles, especially in shallow water. Running aground in seagrass and leaving propeller scars damages the habitat that supports your fishery and is illegal in many areas. Know the rules of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary if you operate there. Collect and recycle used fishing line, which kills birds, turtles and dolphins. Report spills, injured wildlife and violations to the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission at eight eight eight, four zero four, three nine two two.

slides.heading: Reportable marine casualties

items: An unintended grounding, or striking a bridge
Loss of propulsion, steering or control that reduces maneuverability
Anything affecting seaworthiness, such as fire or flooding
A death, or an injury needing treatment beyond first aid
Property damage over $75,000, or significant harm to the environment
Death, or injury beyond first aid

slides.script: As a commercial operator, you must report marine casualties to the Coast Guard. Reportable casualties include an unintended grounding or striking a bridge; a loss of propulsion, steering or control that reduces the boat’s maneuverability; anything that affects the boat’s seaworthiness, such as a fire or flooding; a death; an injury that requires professional medical treatment beyond first aid; property damage over seventy-five thousand dollars; and significant harm to the environment. When in doubt, report it.

slides.heading: How to report

items: Notify the nearest Coast Guard unit immediately
Serious marine incidents also require drug and alcohol testing
Keep your logbook, photos and witness names
Recreational boating accidents are reported to the state instead

slides.script: Report a marine casualty to the nearest Coast Guard sector or station immediately, as soon as you’ve dealt with the emergency. Then file a written report on Form C G twenty-six ninety-two within five days. If the casualty is a serious marine incident, such as one involving a death or serious injury, drug and alcohol testing is also required, with alcohol testing within two hours. Keep your logbook entries, photos and the names of witnesses. Accidents on recreational boats are reported to the state instead.

slides.heading: Drawbridges

items: Request an opening: one prolonged and one short blast, or by radio
Florida bridges usually monitor VHF channel 9
Bridge answers one prolonged and one short: it will open
Five short blasts: it can’t open now
Many bridges open only on a schedule: check 33 CFR 117
It answers with the same signal

slides.script: Florida’s waterways are full of drawbridges. To request an opening, sound one prolonged blast followed by one short blast, or call the bridge tender by radio. Most Florida bridges monitor VHF channel nine. If the bridge will open, it answers with one prolonged and one short blast. If it can’t open right away, it sounds five short blasts. Many bridges open only on a schedule, such as on the hour and half hour, at certain times of day, and the schedules are published in the federal regulations and the Coast Pilot. Hold well back until the bridge is fully open.

slides.heading: Security zones and other rules

items: You’re responsible for your wake and any damage it causes
Naval vessels: minimum speed within 500 yd; no closer than 100 yd
Security zones around cruise ships, tankers and ports

Comply promptly with Coast Guard and FWC boardings

slides.heading: Your plotting kit

items: Parallel rulers or a course plotter
Sharp pencils, an eraser, and a calculator if allowed

slides.script: Welcome to Chart Plotting, the hands-on module. On the exam you’ll work problems on a real training chart, usually NOAA chart twelve ten T R, which covers Martha’s Vineyard to Block Island. Yes, even in Florida. You’ll need parallel rulers or a course plotter, a pair of dividers, sharp pencils, an eraser and, if your exam allows it, a simple calculator. Buy the chart and tools now, bring your own to the exam, and practice with the same ones, so your hands know them by test day.

slides.heading: Walking parallel rulers
slides.script: To find the direction of a line on the chart, line up one edge of the parallel rulers with the line. Then walk the rulers across the chart, holding one ruler down firmly while you swing the other, until an edge passes through the small cross at the center of the compass rose. Read the direction where that edge crosses the rose, on the side in your direction of travel, not the reciprocal side one hundred eighty degrees away. To lay down a course, reverse the process: set the rulers on the rose at your course, then walk them to your position and draw the line.

slides.script: The compass rose has two rings. The outer ring shows true directions, with zero at true north. The inner ring shows magnetic directions, offset by the local variation. The center gives the variation, the year it applied, and the annual change. Reading the inner ring gives you magnetic directions without arithmetic, but the rose may be years out of date, so most captains and most exam problems work in true and convert at the end. Always use the rose nearest the area you’re working in.

slides.heading: Measuring distance
slides.script: Distance is measured on the latitude scale, the one running up the sides of the chart, where one minute of latitude equals one nautical mile. Set the dividers on the two points, then carry them to the side scale at about the same latitude and read the minutes and tenths. On a Mercator chart, the latitude scale stretches as you go north, so always use the part of the scale level with your work. Never measure distance on the longitude scale across the top or bottom of the chart.

slides.heading: Working accurately

items: Keep pencils sharp: a thick line can hide a tenth of a mile
Label every line and position as you go
Work in true; convert to magnetic or compass at the end

slides.script: Plotting rewards neatness. Keep your pencil sharp, because a thick line on a coast chart can hide a tenth of a mile. Label every line and position as you draw it, so you can find your work again in a multi-part problem. Work in true directions and convert to magnetic or compass only at the end. Exam answers are usually to the nearest degree and the nearest tenth of a mile, with choices close together. If your answer doesn’t match any choice, go back and find the step that went wrong rather than guessing.

slides.heading: Reading a position
slides.script: To read a position, measure its latitude on the side scale and its longitude on the top or bottom scale. For latitude, set the dividers from the point to the nearest parallel of latitude, carry them to the side scale and count the minutes, or lay a straightedge horizontally from the point to the scale. For longitude, measure from the nearest meridian to the point, and read the minutes on the top or bottom scale. In west longitude, the numbers increase to the left, and in north latitude, they increase upward. Getting that direction wrong is a common mistake.

slides.script: To plot a position, start with the latitude. Find forty-one degrees, eighteen and a half minutes on the side scale, and lay a straightedge or one arm of your parallel rulers horizontally across the chart at that latitude. Next, find seventy-one degrees, thirty-five minutes on the top scale, set your dividers from the nearest meridian to that longitude, and carry that distance along your straightedge. Mark the spot with a sharp dot, circle it if it’s a fix, and write the time beside it.

slides.heading: Degrees, minutes and tenths

items: Training charts show minutes divided into tenths
41°18.5′ means 41 degrees, 18 and a half minutes
Write latitude first, with N or S; then longitude, with E or W

fig.cap: 41°18.5′ is 41 degrees, 18 and a half minutes
fig.sub: Not 18 minutes 50 seconds. Latitude first, then longitude

slides.script: Each degree has sixty minutes. The training chart’s scales divide each minute into tenths, so positions are written in degrees, minutes and tenths of a minute: forty-one degrees, eighteen point five minutes means eighteen and a half minutes. Don’t confuse that with eighteen minutes, fifty seconds, an older format. Count the small tick marks carefully, since scales at different latitudes may be divided differently. Always write latitude first, with north or south, then longitude, with east or west.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading a light’s position

lines: Lay a straightedge from the light to the side scale

slides.script: Let’s read a light’s position. Lay a straightedge from the light horizontally to the side scale, and read forty-one degrees, ten point two minutes north. Next, measure with the dividers from the nearest meridian, seventy-one degrees thirty minutes west, to the light. Carry that to the top scale, and it spans four point six minutes. Because the light is west of the meridian, and west longitude increases to the west, add: seventy-one degrees thirty-four point six minutes west. The answer is forty-one degrees ten point two north, seventy-one degrees thirty-four point six west.

slides.heading: Labeling a course line
slides.script: Every line you draw gets a label, so you and an examiner can follow your work. Write the course above the line, with a C, the three-digit direction, and T for true or M for magnetic. Write the speed below the line with an S. Mark each position along the track with its symbol, a circle for a fix and a half circle for a dead reckoning position, and write the time beside it, using the twenty-four hour clock. Here, a boat leaves an eight hundred fix on course zero six eight true at twelve knots, with DR positions at nine and ten hundred.

slides.heading: Laying a course, step by step

lines: Draw a line from departure to destination
Walk the rulers to the rose; read the true course
Measure the length with dividers on the latitude scale
Long legs: set dividers to a round distance and step it off
Label course above, speed below; add the ETA at the destination

items: Walk to the rose: true course

slides.script: To lay a course, draw a straight line from your departure point to your destination, checking that it doesn’t cross land or shoals. Walk the parallel rulers to the nearest rose and read the true course on the outer ring. Measure the length of the line with dividers on the latitude scale. For a leg longer than your dividers can span, set them to a round number like one or five miles and step along the line, then measure the leftover piece. Label the line, and write your estimated time of arrival at the destination.

slides.heading: Distance pitfalls

items: 1′ of latitude = 1 nm, measured at the side
Use the part of the scale level with your work
Step carefully: small errors add up on long legs
Answers are usually to the nearest tenth of a mile

a: 1 minute = 1 nautical mile. Use the part level with your work

slides.script: The most common distance errors are measuring on the longitude scale, which gives an answer that’s much too large at Florida or New England latitudes, and using the latitude scale far from where you’re working. A third is careless stepping with the dividers, where small errors add up on a long leg. Work carefully, and give distances to the nearest tenth of a nautical mile.
