slides.heading: 60 D Street

visual.ex: Example: 12 nm at 8 knots takes 60 × 12 ÷ 8 = 90 minutes

els: <circle cx='220' cy='190' r='130' class='s-surfb'/><path d='M90,190 H350 M220,190 V320' class='s-st' stroke-width='2.5'/>
Cover the one you want; the rest is the formula

slides.script: Speed, time and distance problems are free points if you know one formula: sixty times distance equals speed times time. Remember it as sixty D street. Distance is in nautical miles, speed in knots, and time in minutes. To find time, multiply sixty by the distance and divide by the speed. To find distance, multiply speed by time and divide by sixty. To find speed, multiply sixty by the distance and divide by the time. Twelve miles at eight knots takes sixty times twelve, divided by eight, or ninety minutes.

slides.heading: Time arithmetic

lines: Use the 24-hour clock: 1:30 p.m. is 1330
0945 + 50 minutes = 1035 (carry at 60, not 100)
1.75 hours = 1 hour 45 minutes
105 minutes = 1 hour 45 minutes
Multi-leg trips: add the time for each leg

slides.script: Many wrong answers come from time arithmetic, not navigation. Use the twenty-four hour clock, so one thirty in the afternoon is thirteen thirty. When you add minutes, remember there are sixty minutes in an hour, not one hundred: nine forty-five plus fifty minutes is ten thirty-five. Convert decimal hours by multiplying the decimal by sixty, so one point seven five hours is one hour forty-five minutes. For trips with several legs, work out each leg’s time separately and add them.

slides.heading: Finding your ETA

lines: Depart 0815; run 22 nm at 16 knots
Speed changes? Recompute from your latest position
Current changes your speed over ground, and your ETA

els: <circle cx='60' cy='180' r='9' class='s-mag'/><circle cx='380' cy='180' r='9' class='s-mag'/>

slides.script: To find an estimated time of arrival, work out the running time and add it to your departure time. Departing at eight fifteen, running twenty-two miles at sixteen knots takes sixty times twenty-two, divided by sixteen, about eighty-two and a half minutes, or one hour twenty-three minutes. Your ETA is nine thirty-eight. If your speed changes, recompute from your latest position. And remember that current changes your speed over the ground, so a head current makes you late.

slides.heading: Fuel planning

lines: 42 nm out at 14 knots: 3 hours each way
Burning 18 gal/h: 54 gal one way
Rule of thirds: one third out, one third back, one third reserve
Carry 3 × 54 = 162 gallons
Rough seas and heavy loads burn more: stay conservative

els: 3 hours each way at 18 gallons an hour

slides.script: Fuel planning uses the rule of thirds: plan to use one third of your fuel going out, one third coming back, and keep one third in reserve. Say your spot is forty-two miles out, you cruise at fourteen knots, and you burn eighteen gallons an hour. The run out takes three hours and uses fifty-four gallons. By the rule of thirds, you need three times fifty-four, or one hundred sixty-two gallons aboard. Rough seas, head winds and heavy loads all burn more fuel, so be conservative.

slides.heading: Speed through the water vs over the ground

items: Knotmeter or log: speed through the water
The difference is current along your track
Exam problems usually give speed through the water
Find speed over ground from successive fixes

slides.script: Two speeds matter. A knotmeter or log measures your speed through the water. GPS shows your speed over the ground. The difference between them is the current along your track: with a fair current you go faster over the ground, and with a foul current, slower. Exam problems usually give you the boat’s speed through the water, and ask you to find speed over the ground, or speed made good, from fixes or a current diagram.

slides.heading: The correction chain
slides.script: Plotting problems constantly convert between true, magnetic and compass. Remember the chain: true, variation, magnetic, deviation, compass, or True Virgins Make Dull Companions. Going down the chain, from true toward compass, add west and subtract east. Going up the chain, from compass toward true, add east and subtract west. Write each step on paper with its sign, because a single sign error is the most common wrong answer on the plotting exam.

slides.heading: From a plotted course to the course to steer

lines: Plotted course: 068°T
Variation (updated): 14°W
068 + 14 = 082° magnetic
Deviation on 082° from the card: 2°E
082 − 2 = 080° compass: steer 080

slides.script: Here’s the most common conversion. You’ve plotted a course of zero six eight true. The training chart area has variation of about fourteen degrees west. Going from true toward magnetic, add west: zero six eight plus fourteen is zero eight two magnetic. Look up the deviation for that heading on the deviation card, two degrees east. Going from magnetic toward compass, subtract east: zero eight two minus two gives zero eight zero. That’s the course you steer.

slides.script: To plot a bearing taken with the ship’s compass, first convert it to true, using the deviation for the boat’s heading, not for the bearing. Steering zero eight zero by compass, with two degrees east deviation, you see a light bearing zero one five by compass. Add east: zero one seven magnetic. Subtract fourteen west: zero zero three true. Now draw a line through the light in that direction. Your boat lies somewhere along that line, on the side toward you, which runs from the light along the reciprocal, one eight three.

slides.heading: Updating variation

lines: Rose: 14°45′W (2010), annual increase 2′
Change: 16 × 2′ = 32′ increase
Use about 15°W

fig.sub: Update the rose’s variation to the current year

slides.script: The variation printed in the rose applies to the year shown, so update it. Suppose the rose says fourteen degrees forty-five minutes west in twenty ten, increasing two minutes a year. In twenty twenty-six, sixteen years have passed. Sixteen times two minutes is thirty-two minutes of increase. Fourteen forty-five plus thirty-two minutes is fifteen degrees seventeen minutes west, or about fifteen degrees west. Note that many exam questions simply give you the variation to use, so read the question carefully before doing this step.

slides.heading: Common traps

items: Bearings: use the deviation for the boat’s heading
Signs: add west going toward compass; add east going toward true
Reading the wrong side of the rose: 180° off
Mixing true and magnetic in one problem
Answer in what the question asks: true, magnetic or compass
Use the boat’s heading, even for bearings
You read the wrong side of the rose
Answer in what the question asks

slides.script: Watch for these traps. Use the deviation for the boat’s heading when correcting a bearing. Get the signs right: going toward compass, add west; going toward true, add east. Reading the wrong side of the rose puts your answer exactly one hundred eighty degrees off, and that wrong answer is often one of the choices. Don’t mix true and magnetic in the same calculation. And give your answer in whatever the question asks for: true, magnetic or compass.

slides.heading: Lines of position

items: A bearing to a charted object
A range: two charted objects in line
A distance circle: a radar range to a charted point
A depth contour: a rough check
Label: time above the line, bearing below
A bearing to a charted object
A range: two objects in line
A depth contour: a rough check

slides.script: A line of position, or L O P, is a line somewhere along which your boat must be. The most common is a bearing to a charted object, like a lighthouse or tower, converted to true and drawn through the object. Two charted objects in line, a range, give a very accurate L O P with no compass error at all. A radar range to a charted point gives a circle of position around it. Even a depth contour can serve as a rough L O P. Label each one with the time above the line and the true bearing below it.

The most common is a bearing to a charted object, like a lighthouse or tower, converted to true and drawn through the object. Two charted objects in line, a range, give a very accurate L O P with no compass error at all. A radar range to a charted point gives a circle of position around it. Even a depth contour can serve as a rough L O P. Label each one with the time above the line and the true bearing below it.

slides.heading: Two-bearing fix
slides.script: One L O P tells you you’re somewhere on a line. Two L O Ps taken at the same time cross at a point, and that point is a fix. Choose objects whose bearings are about sixty to ninety degrees apart, because when lines cross at a shallow angle, a small bearing error moves the fix a long way. Take the bearings quickly, one after the other, so the boat hasn’t moved much between them. Mark the fix with a small circle and the time.

Take the bearings quickly, one after the other, so the boat hasn’t moved much between them. Mark the fix with a small circle and the time.

slides.heading: Three bearings and the cocked hat
slides.script: A third bearing checks the other two. Because of small errors, three bearings rarely meet at exactly one point. Instead, they form a small triangle, called a cocked hat. Plot your fix in the middle of the triangle. If the triangle is large, something is wrong: a misidentified landmark, a misread compass, a bearing plotted from the wrong side, or a forgotten correction. Recheck before trusting it. The ideal is three objects about one hundred twenty degrees apart.

slides.heading: Other kinds of fixes

items: Bearing and radar range on one object: an excellent fix
Radar ranges to two objects: two circles cross
GPS fix: mark it with a triangle
Cross-check every fix with another source

on one object: an excellent fix

slides.script: Fixes don’t have to come from two bearings. A bearing and a radar range on the same object make an excellent fix, because the two lines cross at right angles. Radar ranges to two separate objects give two circles that cross. A range line plus a bearing on another object works well. An electronic fix from GPS is marked with a small triangle. Whatever the method, cross-check every fix against another source, like the depth, before you trust it.

slides.heading: Plotting symbols
slides.script: Plotting uses standard symbols. A fix, from two or more good lines of position, is a small circle. A dead reckoning position, from course and speed alone, is a half circle drawn on the course line. An estimated position, a DR improved with other information such as current or a single line of position, is a small square. An electronic fix, such as from GPS, is often shown as a triangle. Write the time beside every position, followed by fix, D R or E P.

slides.heading: When to plot a DR

items: At every course or speed change
At the time of every fix or running fix
At the time of a single line of position
Start a new DR track from every fix
At every course or speed change
At every fix or line of position
A new DR track from every fix

slides.script: Dead reckoning follows a few standard rules. Plot a DR position every hour on the hour, at every change of course or speed, at the time of every fix or running fix, and at the time you obtain a single line of position. Whenever you get a fix, start a new DR track from it, because the fix is better information than your old DR. These rules come from Bowditch, the standard navigation reference, and exam problems follow them.

slides.heading: DR versus EP versus fix

items: DR: course and speed only; no current or wind
EP: the DR adjusted with the best other information
EP from one LOP: the point on the LOP nearest the DR
Fix: two or more good LOPs at the same time
Trust a fix over an EP, and an EP over a DR
Two or more good LOPs at one time. Trust it most
The DR adjusted with other information

slides.script: Know the difference between these positions. A DR uses only the course steered and the speed through the water, ignoring current and wind. An estimated position improves on the DR with any other information, such as a known current or a single line of position. With one L O P, the E P is the point on that line nearest your DR position. A fix uses two or more good lines of position taken at the same time. In order of reliability: trust a fix over an E P, and an E P over a DR.

slides.heading: Why DR still matters

items: Keep a log of courses, speeds and times
Your chartplotter track is not a DR
If GPS fails, your last fix plus DR gets you home
A DR shows how much current is pushing you
Practice on calm days and compare with GPS
Your last fix plus DR gets you home
Shows how the current is pushing you

slides.script: With GPS on every boat, why learn dead reckoning? Because electronics fail. If your GPS or power quits, your last fix plus a DR from your logged courses and speeds is how you get home. Keep a written log of course, speed and the times of every change. Your chartplotter track only records where you went; it isn’t a DR. And comparing your DR with a GPS fix shows you exactly how much the current is setting you, which helps you plan the rest of the trip.

slides.heading: The running fix
slides.script: Sometimes only one landmark is in sight. A running fix uses it twice. Take a bearing and plot the line of position. Keep running on a steady course and speed, and later take a second bearing on the same or another object. Then advance the first L O P: move it parallel to itself, in the direction of your course, by the distance you ran between bearings. Where the advanced line crosses the second L O P is your running fix. Its accuracy depends on your course and speed being right, so unknown current between bearings creates error.

lines: 0900: light bears 020°T; course 090°T at 12 knots
0930: the same light bears 330°T
Run between bearings: 12 × 30 ÷ 60 = 6 nm along 090°T
Advance the 0900 LOP 6 nm toward 090°T, keeping it parallel
The 0930 running fix is where it crosses the 0930 LOP

At nine thirty, the same light bears three three zero true. Plot the second L O P. In thirty minutes at twelve knots, you ran six miles along zero nine zero. Pick any point on the nine hundred L O P, measure six miles from it in the direction zero nine zero, and draw a line through that point parallel to the original L O P. Where it crosses the nine thirty L O P is your nine thirty running fix, labeled R fix.

slides.heading: Bow and beam bearings
slides.script: Some special bearings give your distance off without plotting. The bow and beam bearing is the easiest. Note the time when a light is forty-five degrees off your bow, and again when it’s abeam, ninety degrees off the bow. The distance you ran between those two times equals your distance off the light when abeam. This works because the bearings form a right triangle with two equal sides. It’s a quick way to check your distance off a light or a headland.

slides.heading: Doubling the angle on the bow

head: First bearing
Second bearing
Result
rows: Distance off at the 2nd bearing = distance run
Distance off when abeam ≈ 0.7 × distance run
Distance off at the 2nd bearing = distance run

slides.script: Bow and beam is one case of a general rule called doubling the angle on the bow. Whenever an object’s angle on the bow doubles, the distance run between the two bearings equals your distance from the object at the second bearing. With thirty and sixty degrees, the distance run equals your distance off at the sixty degree bearing. A useful extra: with twenty-two and a half and forty-five degrees, your distance off when you pass abeam will be about seven tenths of the distance run, which warns you early if you’ll pass too close.

Run: 18 min at 10 knots = 3 nm

slides.script: Here’s doubling the angle at work. Running at ten knots, you see a light thirty degrees on the bow at ten twelve, and sixty degrees on the bow at ten thirty. In eighteen minutes at ten knots, you ran three miles. So at ten thirty you were three miles from the light. Combine that distance with the ten thirty bearing, and you have a fix: measure three miles from the light along the reciprocal of the bearing, and mark your position.

lessons.title: Current: set, drift and course to steer

slides.heading: Finding set and drift
slides.script: When your fix doesn’t match your dead reckoning position, the difference is current, along with any wind effect or steering error. The set is the direction from the DR position to the fix at the same time. The drift is the distance between them divided by the hours since your last fix. Notice the direction: always from the DR toward the fix. Measuring from the fix back to the DR gives the reciprocal, exactly one hundred eighty degrees wrong, and that wrong answer is almost always one of the choices.

The set is the direction from the DR position to the fix at the same time. The drift is the distance between them divided by the hours since your last fix. Notice the direction: always from the DR toward the fix. Measuring from the fix back to the DR gives the reciprocal, exactly one hundred eighty degrees wrong, and that wrong answer is almost always one of the choices.

slides.heading: Worked example: set and drift

lines: 0800 fix; course 045°T at 8 knots
1000 DR: 16 nm along 045°T
1000 fix lies 2.4 nm from the DR, bearing 120°T from it
Set 120°T; drift 2.4 ÷ 2 = 1.2 knots
Actual track: measure from the 0800 fix to the 1000 fix

slides.script: You leave an eight hundred fix steering zero four five true at eight knots. At ten hundred your DR is sixteen miles along that course, but a ten hundred fix lies two point four miles from the DR, in the direction one two zero true. The set is one two zero true, the direction from DR to fix. The drift is two point four miles divided by two hours, one point two knots. To find what you actually made good, measure the line from the eight hundred fix to the ten hundred fix: that’s your track and speed over the ground.

slides.heading: Course to steer
slides.script: To counter a known current, draw a current diagram. Draw your intended track from the start toward your destination. From the start, draw the current vector: its set and its drift for one hour. From the end of the current vector, set your dividers to your boat speed, and swing an arc until it crosses the intended track. The line from the end of the current vector to that crossing is your course to steer. The distance from the start to the crossing, along the track, is your speed made good.

From the end of the current vector, set your dividers to your boat speed, and swing an arc until it crosses the intended track. The line from the end of the current vector to that crossing is your course to steer. The distance from the start to the crossing, along the track, is your speed made good.

slides.heading: Worked example: course to steer

lines: Intended track 090°T; boat speed 10 knots
Current sets 180°T at 2 knots, pushing you south
Draw 2 nm of current toward 180° from the start
From its end, swing 10 nm to meet the track
Steer about 078°T; speed made good about 9.8 knots

slides.script: Here are numbers. You want to make good a track of zero nine zero true at a boat speed of ten knots, and the current sets one eight zero at two knots, pushing you south. From the start, draw two miles toward one eight zero. From that point, swing ten miles until you hit the track line. The line you just swung runs about zero seven eight true, so you steer zero seven eight, crabbing about twelve degrees into the current. Your speed along the track, the speed made good, is about nine point eight knots.

slides.heading: Quick current rules

items: Current directly with you: add drift to your speed
Wind leeway acts like a current
Add the drift to your speed

slides.script: A few quick rules. A current directly with you adds its drift to your speed, and one directly against you subtracts it, so ten knots against a two knot current makes eight over the ground. A cross current needs a course correction into the current, found with the vector diagram. Wind pushing the boat sideways, called leeway, acts just like a current. And current predictions are only estimates, so keep taking fixes and adjusting your course to steer.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a full exam problem

slides.heading: How the plotting exam works

items: A set of questions worked on the training chart
Questions often build on each other
An early mistake can carry through
Keep a scratch sheet with every step

fig.sub: Questions build on each other: keep a scratch sheet of every step

slides.script: The plotting exam is a set of questions you work on the training chart, and you need seventy percent to pass. The questions often build on each other, like a real voyage: you plot a departure, lay a course, take bearings, find a fix, work out the current, and compute an arrival time. That means an early mistake can carry through several answers. Keep a scratch sheet showing every step, so you can find an error quickly. Let’s walk through a complete problem.

Next, lay a course to the next mark and read zero six eight true from the rose. The question gives variation fifteen west and deviation two east, so the compass course is zero six eight plus fifteen minus two: zero eight one. The leg measures nine point six miles; at twelve knots, that’s forty-eight minutes, for an ETA of seven forty-eight.

slides.heading: Step 3: correct for the current

lines: From the 0730 fix, lay a new course to the mark
Draw a current diagram with set 160°T, drift 1.6 knots
Find the course to steer and speed made good
Convert the course to compass for the helmsman
Recompute the ETA using speed made good

items: Course to steer and speed made good
Convert to compass; recompute the ETA

slides.script: Step three. From the seven thirty fix, lay a new course line to the mark. Then draw a current diagram, with the current setting one six zero at one point six knots, to find the course to steer that keeps you on that line, and your speed made good along it. Convert the course to steer to a compass course, using the variation and the deviation for the new heading. Finally, measure the remaining distance and divide by the speed made good, not your boat speed, to get the new ETA.

slides.heading: Final exam tips

items: Read each question twice: true, magnetic or compass?
Use the variation the question gives you
Show your work so you can find mistakes
Off by 180°? You read the wrong side of the rose
Drill every day in Plotting drills

slides.script: That’s the end of the course. A few final tips. Read every question twice and note whether it asks for true, magnetic or compass. Use the variation the question gives you, rather than the chart’s rose, when one is given. Show your work so you can find mistakes. If your answer is off by exactly one hundred eighty degrees, you read the wrong side of the rose or reversed a set. And use the plotting drills in this app every day until the calculations are automatic. You’ve now covered every module of the exam. Good luck, Captain.

questions.text: (BOTH) The white light showing over an arc of 225° is the:
questions.explanation: The masthead light shines from dead ahead to 22.5° abaft each beam: 225° total.

questions.text: (INLAND) A power-driven vessel leaving a dock or berth sounds:
questions.explanation: Inland Rule 34(g): one prolonged blast when leaving a dock or berth.

questions.text: (BOTH) The danger or doubt signal is:
questions.explanation: Rule 34(d): at least five short and rapid blasts when you don’t understand the other vessel’s intentions.

questions.text: (BOTH) In a crossing situation, the stand-on vessel shall:
questions.explanation: Rule 17: the stand-on vessel keeps course and speed, though she may act if the give-way vessel isn’t taking action.

questions.text: (BOTH) Your power boat is overtaking a vessel engaged in fishing. Who keeps clear?
questions.explanation: Rule 13 overrides Rule 18: the overtaking vessel always keeps clear.

questions.text: (BOTH) All-round green over white lights indicate a vessel:
(BOTH) The day shape for a vessel at anchor is:
questions.explanation: Rule 30: one ball in the fore part of the vessel.

questions.text: (INTERNATIONAL) Two short blasts mean:
options: I am altering my course to port
I intend to leave you on my starboard side
questions.explanation: International signals announce action being taken. Two short = altering course to port.

questions.text: (BOTH) In fog you hear two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes. It is:
options: A power-driven vessel underway but stopped
questions.explanation: Rule 35(b): two prolonged blasts = power-driven vessel underway, not making way.

questions.text: (BOTH) Which is NOT a factor in determining safe speed?
questions.explanation: Rule 6 lists visibility, traffic, maneuverability, background lights, wind, sea, current and draft vs depth.

questions.text: (INLAND) Meeting head-on, one short blast means:
options: I intend to leave you on my port side
I am altering course to starboard
I intend to leave you on my starboard side
questions.explanation: Inland signals state intentions and need an answer. One short = port-to-port passing.

questions.text: (BOTH) Two sailing vessels are crossing with the wind on different sides. Which keeps clear?
options: The one with the wind on her port side
The one with the wind on her starboard side
questions.explanation: Rule 12: the vessel with the wind on the port side keeps clear.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel under 20 m in a narrow channel shall not:
options: Impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel

questions.text: (BOTH) All-round lights red, white, red in a vertical line mean a vessel:
options: Restricted in her ability to maneuver
questions.explanation: Red-white-red = RAM. Day shape: ball, diamond, ball.

questions.text: (BOTH) Each sidelight shows over an arc of:
questions.explanation: From dead ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam on its own side.

questions.text: (INTERNATIONAL) Three all-round red lights in a vertical line mean a vessel:
questions.explanation: Constrained by draft exists only in the International rules. Day shape: a cylinder.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel under 100 m at anchor in fog sounds:
options: A rapid bell for about 5 seconds every minute

questions.text: (BOTH) At night you’re approaching a vessel and can see only her white sternlight. You are:
questions.explanation: Seeing only the sternlight means you’re more than 22.5° abaft her beam: overtaking.

questions.text: (INLAND) On the Western Rivers, which power-driven vessel has the right of way?
options: The one proceeding downbound with the current
questions.explanation: Inland Rule 14(d) and 9(a)(ii): the downbound vessel has the right of way and proposes the manner of passing.

questions.text: (BOTH) Risk of collision is deemed to exist when:
options: The compass bearing doesn’t change appreciably and the range decreases
The other vessel sounds one blast

questions.text: (BOTH) Two all-round red lights in a vertical line indicate a vessel:
options: Restricted in her ability to maneuver
questions.explanation: “Red over red, the captain is dead.” Sidelights are added when making way.

questions.text: (BOTH) All-round red over white lights indicate a vessel:
options: Engaged in fishing other than trawling

questions.text: (BOTH) All-round white over red lights indicate:
(BOTH) Your power boat and a sailboat under sail alone are crossing. Who gives way?
options: The vessel on the other’s starboard side
questions.explanation: Rule 18: a power-driven vessel keeps clear of a sailing vessel (unless the sailboat is overtaking).

questions.text: (BOTH) Two power-driven vessels meet head-on. What do they do?
options: The one with the current stands on
questions.explanation: Rule 14: each alters course to starboard and passes port to port.

questions.text: (BOTH) Two power-driven vessels are crossing. The give-way vessel is the one that:
options: Has the other on her own starboard side
Has the other on her own port side

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel is overtaking when coming up on another from a direction more than:
(BOTH) The sternlight shows over an arc of:
(BOTH) The towing light is:
options: Yellow, with the same arc as the sternlight
questions.explanation: Rule 21(d): yellow, 135°, placed above the sternlight.

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel also using her engine shows by day:
questions.explanation: Rule 25(e). She is a power-driven vessel under the rules.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel aground shows at night:
options: Anchor light(s) plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line

questions.text: (INTERNATIONAL) In a narrow channel, the signal “I intend to overtake you on your starboard side” is:
questions.explanation: Rule 34(c). The vessel being overtaken agrees with prolonged-short-prolonged-short.

questions.text: (BOTH) A prolonged blast lasts about:
(BOTH) In restricted visibility, a sailing vessel underway sounds every 2 minutes:
questions.explanation: Rule 35(c), also used by fishing, towing, NUC and RAM vessels.

questions.text: (INLAND) Passing agreements may be made by radio on the bridge-to-bridge channel:
(BOTH) Action taken to avoid collision should be:
options: Positive, made in ample time, and large enough to be readily apparent
A series of small course changes
Taken only after sounding the danger signal
Taken only by the stand-on vessel

questions.text: Red nun buoys carry:
questions.explanation: Red marks are even-numbered; green marks are odd.

questions.text: An isolated danger mark is colored:
questions.explanation: It sits on a small danger with navigable water all around. Topmark: two black balls.

questions.text: A tidal current flowing toward shore is called:
questions.explanation: Flood runs toward land; ebb runs away from it.

questions.text: Deviation is caused by:
questions.explanation: Deviation varies with heading and is found on the boat’s deviation card.

questions.text: A light described as “Oc” is:
options: Lit longer than it is dark
Dark longer than it is lit
questions.explanation: Occulting = mostly on with brief eclipses.

questions.text: Neap tides occur at:
questions.explanation: Neap tides have the smallest range. Spring tides come at new and full moon.

questions.text: The light on a safe water mark is:
questions.explanation: Safe water marks are red and white vertical stripes with a white Mo(A) light.

questions.text: A green daybeacon is shaped like a:
Depths on U.S. charts are measured from:
questions.explanation: MLLW, so actual depth is usually at least what’s charted.

questions.text: On the ICW, a yellow square on any mark means:
options: Treat it as a green (port-hand) mark
Treat it as a red mark
questions.explanation: Yellow square = can; yellow triangle = nun, regardless of the mark’s own color.

questions.text: Under the rule of twelfths, the tide rises fastest during:
A rapidly falling barometer means:
questions.explanation: Rapid falls signal a strong low-pressure system and rising wind.

questions.text: Entering a harbor from sea, you see green can buoy “7.” You leave it on your:
questions.explanation: Red right returning, so green stays on your left.

questions.text: A buoy with red and white vertical stripes marks:
options: Safe water, often a channel entrance
questions.explanation: Safe water marks have navigable water all around.

questions.text: On the ICW, a green can buoy with a yellow triangle should be treated as:
questions.explanation: Where ICW and another channel share marks, the yellow symbol tells ICW traffic which side.

questions.text: A light described as “Q R” is:
options: Red, quick flashing, about 60 flashes per minute

questions.text: Spring tides occur at:
questions.explanation: Sun and moon align, giving the largest range.

questions.text: Magnetic variation is found:
questions.explanation: The rose shows variation, the year, and the annual change.

questions.text: A preferred channel mark should be treated as:
options: The color of its top band
The color of its bottom band
questions.explanation: The top band shows which side of the preferred channel it marks.

questions.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, with your back to the wind, low pressure is:
“Fl G 4s” on a chart means:
options: A green light flashing every 4 seconds

questions.text: Following the ICW “returning” direction on Florida’s Atlantic coast, you are heading:
questions.explanation: The ICW convention runs clockwise around the U.S.: south along the Atlantic coast, then west along the Gulf.

questions.text: A sea breeze typically:
options: Blows from sea toward land on warm afternoons
Blows from land toward sea at night
questions.explanation: Land heats faster than water, drawing cooler sea air ashore.

questions.text: A Class C fire involves:
questions.explanation: De-energize first; use CO2 or dry chemical.

questions.text: The VHF distress, safety and calling channel is:
questions.explanation: Channel 16. DSC distress alerts go out on channel 70.

questions.text: The best first treatment for a hypothermic person is to:
options: Remove wet clothes and gently warm the core
Put them straight into a hot shower
questions.explanation: Rewarm the core gently; rubbing limbs or rapid warming can send cold blood to the heart.

questions.text: An OUPV holder may carry at most how many passengers for hire on an uninspected vessel?
questions.explanation: That limit is where the “six-pack” name comes from.

questions.text: Moving weight higher on a boat:
questions.explanation: A higher center of gravity reduces the righting arm.

questions.text: “PASS” for using an extinguisher stands for:
questions.explanation: Aim at the base of the fire.

questions.text: “Pan-pan” is used for:
options: An urgent situation without immediate danger to life
questions.explanation: Mayday is distress; pan-pan is urgency; securité is safety.

questions.text: Oil spills must be reported to:
The MARPOL garbage placard is required on boats:
questions.explanation: So is the oil discharge placard.

questions.text: The preferred anchor scope in normal conditions is:
questions.explanation: 5:1 minimum, 7:1 preferred, more in heavy weather.

questions.text: A gasoline fire in the bilge is fought with:
questions.explanation: Class B, flammable liquids. Water spreads it.

questions.text: Water depth 12 ft, bow 3 ft above the water. How much rode for 7:1 scope?
Free surface effect in a partly filled tank:
questions.explanation: Sloshing liquid acts like raising the center of gravity.

questions.text: A friend voluntarily chips in his share of the actual fuel cost of a fishing trip. Under federal law he is:
options: Not a passenger for hire: voluntary sharing of actual expenses isn’t consideration
questions.explanation: 46 U.S.C. 2101 excludes voluntary sharing of a voyage’s actual expenses from “consideration.” A required payment as a condition of the trip would make him a passenger for hire.

questions.text: A passenger has hot, red, dry skin and is confused. This is most likely:
questions.explanation: Cool them immediately and call for help.

questions.text: Plastic may be thrown overboard:
questions.explanation: MARPOL Annex V prohibits discharging plastic everywhere.

questions.text: “Mayday” means:
options: Grave and imminent danger requiring immediate help
A request for a radio check
questions.explanation: Repeat it three times, then give vessel, position, problem and number aboard.

questions.text: A modern EPIRB transmits on:
questions.explanation: Register it with NOAA so rescuers know who you are.

questions.text: The first actions when someone falls overboard are:
options: Shout, point and keep eyes on them, and throw flotation
Call the Coast Guard before anything else
Turn away from the side they fell
questions.explanation: Then press MOB on the GPS and maneuver back, swinging the stern clear.

questions.text: Carrying 7 or more passengers for hire requires:
options: An inspected vessel with a Certificate of Inspection and a Master license
questions.explanation: The OUPV limit is 6 passengers on uninspected vessels.

questions.text: A written waste management plan is required on ocean-going boats:
options: 40 ft and over with a galley and berthing

questions.text: A marine casualty report on Form CG-2692 must be filed within:
questions.explanation: Notify the Coast Guard immediately; the written form follows within 5 days.

questions.text: Nylon line is often chosen for anchor rode because it:
A boat with a quick, snappy roll is described as:
questions.explanation: A slow, lazy roll means low stability (tender).

questions.text: How long to run 18 nm at 12 knots?
Compass course 135°, deviation 3°E, variation 7°W. What is the true course?
On a chart, distance is measured on the:
At 20 knots for 24 minutes you cover:
One minute of latitude equals:
questions.explanation: A nautical mile is about 6,076 ft.

questions.text: True course 090°, variation 6°W, deviation 2°W. What compass course do you steer?
You ran 15 nm in 50 minutes. What was your speed?
After 3 hours, your fix is 4.5 nm at 180°T from your DR position. What are the set and drift?
questions.explanation: Set is measured from DR to fix. Drift = 4.5 ÷ 3.

questions.text: Running 42 nm out at 14 knots, burning 18 gal/hr. By the rule of thirds, how much fuel do you carry?
questions.explanation: 3 hours × 18 = 54 gal one way. One-third out, one-third back, one-third reserve: 162.

questions.text: A light bears 45° off your bow at 1010 and is abeam at 1025. At 12 knots, how far off is it when abeam?
questions.explanation: Bow-and-beam bearing: distance run (15 min at 12 kn = 3 nm) equals distance off.

questions.text: Chart variation is 5°30′W (2020), decreasing 6′ per year. What do you use in 2026?
On a plot, a dead reckoning position is marked with:
questions.explanation: A fix is a full circle; an estimated position is often a square.

questions.text: For the most accurate two-bearing fix, the bearing lines should cross at about:
questions.explanation: Shallow crossing angles magnify small bearing errors.

questions.text: (INLAND) The Inland Navigation Rules apply to:
options: All vessels on the inland waters of the United States
questions.explanation: Inland Rule 1. They also apply to U.S. vessels on Canadian Great Lakes waters where they don’t conflict with Canadian law.

questions.text: On a chart, the boundary between Inland and International waters is the:
questions.explanation: Demarcation lines are printed as dashed magenta lines and listed in 33 CFR Part 80.

questions.text: (BOTH) Rule 2 permits departure from the rules when:
(BOTH) Distress signals are described in:
questions.explanation: Annex IV lists the distress signals referred to in Rule 37.

questions.text: (BOTH) Additional signals for fishing vessels fishing in close proximity are in:
questions.explanation: Annex II covers trawlers shooting and hauling nets, nets fast on obstructions, and purse seiners.

questions.text: (BOTH) Special rules made by a local authority for a harbor or river must:
options: Conform as closely as possible to the Navigation Rules
Be approved by every vessel owner

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel of special construction that can’t fully comply with the light rules shall:
options: Comply as closely as possible, as her government determines
questions.explanation: Rule 1(e). Inland, this is a certificate of alternative compliance.

questions.text: (BOTH) Under Rule 2, being the stand-on vessel:
options: Doesn’t excuse you from acting to avoid collision
Lets you hold course in every situation
Means the other vessel is always at fault
questions.explanation: Nothing in the rules excuses neglect of ordinary seamanship.

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailboat with sails up and engine running is a:
options: Vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
questions.explanation: A sailing vessel is under sail with propelling machinery, if fitted, not being used.

questions.text: (BOTH) A charter boat trolling lines is:
options: A power-driven vessel, not “engaged in fishing”
A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel is “underway” when she is not:
options: At anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground
questions.explanation: Rule 3(i). A drifting vessel is underway.

questions.text: (BOTH) A boat drifting with her engine off is:
questions.explanation: She isn’t anchored, made fast or aground, but isn’t moving through the water under her own power.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel whose steering has failed is:
options: Restricted in her ability to maneuver
questions.explanation: An exceptional circumstance, not the nature of her work.

questions.text: (BOTH) A dredge working in a channel is:
options: Restricted in her ability to maneuver
A power-driven vessel with no special status
questions.explanation: Dredging is listed in the definition of RAM.

questions.text: The category “constrained by her draft” exists:
questions.explanation: Inland rules have no constrained-by-draft category.

questions.text: (BOTH) Vessels are “in sight of one another” only when:
options: One can be observed visually from the other
Each appears on the other’s radar

questions.text: (BOTH) Which is NOT restricted visibility?
questions.explanation: Restricted visibility comes from fog, mist, snow, heavy rain, sandstorms and similar causes.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel engaged in diving operations is classed as:
options: Restricted in her ability to maneuver
questions.explanation: Underwater operations are listed in the definition of RAM.

questions.text: (BOTH) Rules 4 through 10 apply:
questions.explanation: Section I of the steering rules.

questions.text: (BOTH) A proper lookout must be kept:
(BOTH) Safe speed is determined by:
options: Conditions such as visibility, traffic and your vessel’s maneuverability
questions.explanation: Rule 6 lists factors, not a number.

questions.text: (BOTH) For vessels with operational radar, which is a safe-speed factor?
options: The possibility that small vessels may not be detected at adequate range
The color of the radar display
How long you’ve owned the radar

questions.text: (BOTH) Assumptions shall not be made on the basis of:
options: Scanty information, especially scanty radar information

questions.text: (BOTH) Risk of collision may exist even with an appreciable bearing change when approaching:
options: A very large vessel, a tow, or any vessel at close range

questions.text: (BOTH) An alteration of course alone may be the most effective action if it:
options: Is made in good time, is substantial, and doesn’t create another close-quarters situation
Is made at the last moment

questions.text: (BOTH) To avoid collision or gain time to assess the situation, a vessel shall if necessary:
options: Slacken her speed or take all way off

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel required not to impede another shall:
options: Take early action to leave sea room for the other’s safe passage
Stand on until the last moment
Sound the danger signal and hold course

questions.text: (BOTH) In a narrow channel, a vessel shall keep:
options: As near the outer limit on her starboard side as is safe and practicable
In the center of the channel
On the port side of the channel

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel in a narrow channel shall not:
options: Impede a vessel that can safely navigate only within the channel

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel engaged in fishing in a narrow channel:
options: Shall not impede any other vessel navigating within the channel
Has right of way over all vessels
Must leave the channel at night

questions.text: (BOTH) Nearing a bend where other vessels may be hidden, you sound:
questions.explanation: Rule 9(f). A vessel around the bend answers with one prolonged blast.

questions.text: (BOTH) Anchoring in a narrow channel:
options: Should be avoided if circumstances admit
Is allowed only for fishing vessels

questions.text: (INLAND) On the Western Rivers, a power-driven vessel proceeding upbound against the current:
options: Holds as necessary to permit safe passing
questions.explanation: Inland Rule 9: the downbound vessel has the right of way.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel obliged to cross a traffic lane does so:
options: On a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the traffic flow
At a small angle to the traffic flow
Only at the end of the lane

questions.text: (BOTH) Which vessels may use an inshore traffic zone?
options: Vessels under 20 m, sailing vessels and fishing vessels

questions.text: (BOTH) Joining a traffic lane from the side should be done:
options: At as small an angle to the general direction of traffic as practicable

questions.text: (BOTH) Rules 11 through 18 apply to vessels:
options: In restricted visibility, not in sight

questions.text: (BOTH) Two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side. Which keeps clear?
(BOTH) A port-tack vessel can’t tell which tack a vessel to windward is on. She shall:
options: Keep out of the way of the other
Sound five short blasts and stand on

questions.text: (BOTH) For Rule 12, the windward side is:
options: The side opposite to that on which the mainsail is carried
The side the mainsail is carried on

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel overtaking a power-driven vessel:
options: Has right of way because she is sailing

questions.text: (BOTH) In doubt whether you are overtaking, you shall:
options: Assume you are overtaking and act accordingly

questions.text: (BOTH) After you begin overtaking, the bearing changes and you end up on the other vessel’s beam. You are:
options: Still the overtaking vessel until finally past and clear

questions.text: (BOTH) At night, a vessel overtaking another would see:
options: Her masthead light and one sidelight

questions.text: (BOTH) A head-on situation at night exists when you see the other vessel’s:
options: Masthead lights in line and/or both sidelights

questions.text: (BOTH) In a crossing situation, the give-way vessel shall, if circumstances admit:
options: Avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel

questions.text: (BOTH) The give-way vessel shall:
options: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear

questions.text: (BOTH) The stand-on vessel MAY act by her maneuver alone when:
options: It becomes apparent the give-way vessel isn’t taking appropriate action
She sees the other’s green sidelight

questions.text: (BOTH) The stand-on vessel SHALL act when:
options: Collision can’t be avoided by the give-way vessel’s action alone
She first sights the other vessel
The give-way vessel sounds one blast

questions.text: (BOTH) A power-driven stand-on vessel acting in a crossing situation should not, if circumstances permit:
options: Alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side

questions.text: (INLAND) On the Western Rivers, a power-driven vessel crossing the river keeps out of the way of:
options: A power-driven vessel ascending or descending the river
No one; she has right of way

questions.text: (BOTH) In doubt whether a head-on situation exists, a vessel shall:
options: Assume it does and act accordingly

questions.text: (BOTH) A power-driven vessel underway keeps out of the way of:
options: Vessels not under command, restricted, engaged in fishing, and sailing
questions.explanation: Rule 18(a), except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require.

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel underway keeps out of the way of:
options: A power-driven vessel crossing her bow

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel engaged in fishing keeps out of the way, so far as possible, of:
options: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver

questions.text: (INTERNATIONAL) Vessels other than NUC and RAM shall, if circumstances admit, avoid impeding:
options: A vessel constrained by her draft

questions.text: (BOTH) Rule 18 applies except where which rules otherwise require?
questions.explanation: Narrow channels, traffic separation schemes and overtaking.

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel overtaking a vessel engaged in fishing:
options: Keeps clear, because she is overtaking
Stands on, because she is sailing

questions.text: (BOTH) A seaplane on the water shall, in general:
options: Keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding them
Have right of way over all vessels
Be treated as a sailing vessel

questions.text: (INLAND) Which category does NOT exist under Inland rules?
questions.explanation: Constrained by draft is International only.

questions.text: (BOTH) Rule 19 applies to vessels:
options: Not in sight of one another, in or near restricted visibility
In sight of one another in fog

questions.text: (BOTH) In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel shall:
options: Have her engines ready for immediate maneuver
Increase speed to clear the area

questions.text: (BOTH) Under Rule 19:
options: There is no stand-on or give-way vessel
The vessel to starboard stands on
questions.explanation: Every vessel shares the duty to avoid collision.

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel detected by radar alone is forward of your beam and not being overtaken. Avoid:
options: An alteration of course to port
An alteration of course to starboard

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel detected by radar alone is abaft your beam. Avoid:
options: An alteration of course toward it

questions.text: (BOTH) Hearing a fog signal apparently forward of the beam (risk not ruled out), you shall:
options: Reduce to the minimum speed at which you can keep your course
Sound five short blasts and hold speed

questions.text: (BOTH) If necessary after hearing a fog signal forward of the beam, a vessel shall:
(BOTH) When two vessels in fog come into sight of one another:
options: The rules for vessels in sight, 11 to 18, apply
questions.explanation: Rule 19 applies only while they are not in sight.

questions.text: (BOTH) Navigation lights shall be shown:
options: From sunset to sunrise, and in restricted visibility

questions.text: (BOTH) The masthead light of a vessel 50 m or more must be visible at least:
(BOTH) Sidelights on a vessel under 12 m must be visible at least:
(BOTH) The masthead light of a vessel 12 m or more but under 20 m must be visible at least:
(BOTH) A second masthead light, abaft and higher than the forward one, is required on power-driven vessels:
questions.explanation: Rule 23. Vessels under 50 m may show one.

questions.text: (BOTH) A power-driven vessel under 7 m with a top speed of 7 knots or less may show:
options: An all-round white light, and sidelights if practicable

questions.text: (BOTH) An air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode adds:
(BOTH) A “flashing light” flashes at:
questions.explanation: Rule 21. Inland’s special flashing light is 50 to 70 per minute.

questions.text: (INLAND) On the Great Lakes, a power-driven vessel may show an all-round white light in place of:
options: The second masthead light and the sternlight

questions.text: (BOTH) A power-driven vessel towing astern, tow 200 m or less, shows:
options: Two masthead lights in a vertical line
Three masthead lights in a vertical line

questions.text: (BOTH) When the tow exceeds 200 m, the towing vessel shows:
options: Three masthead lights in a vertical line

questions.text: (BOTH) The length of a tow is measured:
options: From the stern of the towing vessel to the after end of the tow
From the bow of the towing vessel to the stern of the tow
From the towing light to the tow’s sternlight

questions.text: (BOTH) The towing light is:
options: Yellow, above the sternlight, with the same arc

questions.text: (BOTH) A diamond shape is shown when:
options: The tow exceeds 200 m, on both the towing vessel and the tow

questions.text: (INLAND) A power-driven vessel pushing ahead shows aft:
options: Two towing lights in a vertical line
A towing light over a sternlight

questions.text: (INLAND) A vessel being pushed ahead (not a composite unit) shows at the forward end:
options: Sidelights and a special flashing light

questions.text: (BOTH) A pushing vessel and pushed vessel rigidly connected as a composite unit show:
options: The lights of a single power-driven vessel

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel towing another in distress, unable to show towing lights, should:
options: Indicate the relationship, such as by illuminating the towline

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel underway shows:
options: A masthead light, sidelights and a sternlight

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel under 20 m may combine her sidelights and sternlight:
options: In one lantern at or near the top of the mast

questions.text: (BOTH) The optional all-round masthead lights of a sailing vessel are:
options: Red over green, not shown with a tricolor

questions.text: (INLAND) A sailing vessel under 12 m, under sail and power by day:
options: Isn’t required to show the cone, but may
Must show a cone, apex up

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel engaged in trawling shows:
(BOTH) A vessel fishing (not trawling) with gear extending more than 150 m adds:
options: An all-round white light in the direction of the gear
A red light at the stern

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel engaged in fishing but not making way shows:
options: Her fishing lights, without sidelights or sternlight
questions.explanation: Sidelights and sternlight are added only when making way.

questions.text: (BOTH) Under Annex II, a trawler hauling her nets may show:
questions.explanation: Shooting nets: two white. Net fast: two red.

questions.text: (BOTH) A sailing vessel under 7 m that doesn’t show sidelights and sternlight must:
options: Have a white torch or lantern ready to show in time

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel not under command and making way shows:
options: Two all-round red lights plus sidelights and sternlight

questions.text: (BOTH) A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, at anchor, shows:
options: Her RAM lights plus anchor lights

questions.text: (BOTH) A dredge marks the side on which another vessel may pass with:
options: Two all-round green lights in a vertical line
questions.explanation: Rule 27. Two reds mark the obstruction.

questions.text: (BOTH) A small vessel engaged in diving operations shows a rigid replica of code flag A at least:
(BOTH) A vessel engaged in mine clearance means it is dangerous to approach within:
